RP-01.title: Why Do We Yawn?
RP-01.text:
Everyone yawns, from newborn babies to great-grandparents. Even dogs, cats, and fish yawn. Yet scientists still argue about why.

For many years, the most popular explanation was that yawning brings extra oxygen into the body. A tired brain, the story went, needs a big gulp of air. However, when researchers had volunteers breathe air with extra oxygen, the volunteers yawned just as often as before. The oxygen idea did not hold up.

A newer idea is that yawning helps cool the brain. When we yawn, we stretch the jaw and pull in a large breath of air, which may increase blood flow and carry heat away from the head. Supporters point out that people tend to yawn less when the air outside is very hot, when a deep breath would not cool anything.

Yawning is also contagious. Seeing, hearing, or even reading about a yawn can trigger one. Some researchers believe contagious yawning is linked to empathy, our ability to share the feelings of others, because people tend to catch yawns more often from family and friends than from strangers.

None of these explanations has been proven beyond doubt. For now, the humble yawn remains one of the body's small mysteries. (Did you yawn while reading this?)

RP-02.title: Preparing for Your Fasting Blood Test
RP-02.text:
Your provider has ordered a fasting blood test. Fasting means no food or drink except water for a set time before the test. Follow these steps so your results are accurate.

1. Schedule your blood draw for the morning if you can. Most of your fasting time will then happen while you sleep.
2. Stop eating and drinking anything except water 12 hours before your appointment. For an 8:00 a.m. appointment, your last meal should end by 8:00 p.m. the night before.
3. Keep drinking plain water. Water makes your veins easier to find.
4. Do not chew gum, smoke, or exercise hard during the fasting period. These can change your results.
5. Take your usual medicines with water unless your provider told you to stop them. If you take insulin or another diabetes medicine, call your provider before you fast.
6. Bring a snack to eat right after your blood is drawn.

If you eat by mistake during the fasting period, call the lab. You may need to reschedule.

RP-05.title: Two Views on Later School Start Times
RP-05.text:
Passage A (written by a pediatrician)
Teenagers are not lazy; their body clocks are different. During puberty, the brain begins releasing the sleep hormone melatonin later at night, so most teens cannot fall asleep before about 11 p.m. When school starts at 7:30 a.m., many students are in class on six hours of sleep or less. Districts that have moved start times later have reported better attendance and fewer car crashes involving teen drivers. Starting high school at 8:30 a.m. or later is a simple change that protects students' health.

Passage B (written by a parent and bus company owner)
Later start times sound good, but the details matter. In our county, the same buses carry elementary, middle, and high school students in shifts. If high schools start later, either the youngest children wait at bus stops in the dark or the district must buy more buses and hire more drivers, which costs money that could go to teachers. Later dismissal also pushes after-school jobs and sports practices into the evening. Before changing the schedule, our district should study what the change would cost and who would pay.

RP-06.title: Letter to the Editor: Get Sugary Drinks Out of Our Hospital
RP-06.text:
To the Editor:

Last week I visited my father at Bayside General Hospital (a fictional hospital). In the lobby, a vending machine full of sodas and sweetened teas stood right beside a poster about preventing diabetes. Nothing could be more ridiculous.

A 20-ounce bottle of regular soda contains about 16 teaspoons of sugar. The American Heart Association recommends that most women limit added sugar to about 6 teaspoons a day and most men to about 9. Several hospitals across the country have already stopped selling sugary drinks, and their stores still make money selling water, milk, and unsweetened tea.

Hospitals are supposed to protect health. Every hospital administrator who keeps these machines stocked is simply putting profit ahead of patients. Bayside should remove sugary drinks this year and show our community what healthy choices look like.

— A concerned visitor

RP-07.title: First Shift
RP-07.text:
Dana arrived at the nursing home twenty minutes early, her new scrubs still creased from the package. The charge nurse, Ms. Okafor, handed her a clipboard and a list of eight residents.

By ten o'clock Dana had helped three residents dress, refilled water pitchers, and recorded every meal in the chart. At eleven, Mr. Bell in room 14 refused his lunch. Dana remembered her instructor's advice to ask rather than assume. She pulled up a chair and asked what was wrong. Mr. Bell admitted that his dentures hurt and that the sandwich was too hard to chew.

Dana reported the problem to Ms. Okafor, who called the kitchen. Twenty minutes later, a bowl of soup and soft bread arrived. Mr. Bell ate every bite.

At the end of the shift, Ms. Okafor stopped Dana at the time clock. "You noticed something the rest of us missed," she said. "That's what this job is really about." Dana drove home tired, but she was already looking forward to tomorrow.

RP-08.title: The Nurse Who Used Numbers
RP-08.text:
Florence Nightingale is famous as the founder of modern nursing, but she was also a pioneer in using statistics to change policy.

In 1854, during the Crimean War, Nightingale and a team of nurses arrived at a British army hospital in Scutari, in present-day Turkey. The hospital was overcrowded and filthy, and far more soldiers were dying of diseases such as cholera and typhus than of battle wounds.

Nightingale kept careful records. After the war, she worked with statisticians to analyze the death rates. To make her findings impossible to ignore, she created colorful circular charts showing that most of the deaths had been caused by preventable disease. Her charts helped persuade government officials to improve sanitation in military hospitals.

In 1859 she published Notes on Nursing, a short book that stressed fresh air, clean water, and cleanliness. In 1860 she helped establish a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London. Today, many nurses still see her as a model of how careful observation and clear evidence can improve patient care.

RP-09.title: The Bay's Living Filters
RP-09.text:
Oysters do more than end up on a dinner plate. In the Chesapeake Bay, they act as natural water filters. An oyster feeds by pumping water over its gills and trapping tiny bits of algae and sediment. A single adult oyster can filter as much as 50 gallons of water in a day.

Cleaner water lets more sunlight reach the bottom of the bay, where underwater grasses grow. These grasses shelter young crabs and fish. Oyster reefs also provide hiding places for many small animals, so a healthy reef supports a whole community of life.

Over the past two centuries, the bay's oyster population fell sharply because of overharvesting, disease, and pollution. With fewer oysters to filter it, the water became cloudier. For decades, and on a much larger scale since the 2010s, government agencies, watermen, and volunteer groups have worked to restore oyster reefs by planting young oysters on new reef sites in several rivers.

Restoration takes time. An oyster needs about two to three years to reach market size, and a reef can take many years to become fully established. Still, many scientists see reef restoration as one of the most promising ways to improve the bay's health.

RP-14.title: Two Short Stories About Trying Again
RP-14.text:
Story A: The Bridge
Marisol lost the bridge-building contest in seventh grade when her popsicle-stick bridge snapped under the first weight. She studied the broken pieces for a week, then noticed that every break had happened where the glue joints were longest. The next year she shortened the joints and added triangles to the frame. Her bridge held twice the weight of any other entry.

Story B: The Garden
Every spring, Mr. Lyle planted tomatoes along the fence, and every summer the plants wilted before they fruited. His neighbor suggested that the fence blocked the afternoon sun. Mr. Lyle grumbled that tomatoes had always grown there when his wife was alive. That year, the plants wilted again. The next spring, he carried his seedlings to the sunny corner of the yard, and by August he was giving tomatoes away to the whole street.

RP-15.title: How to Make a Simple Saline Rinse for a Sore Throat
RP-15.text:
A warm salt-water gargle can soothe a sore throat. Here is how to make one.

First, wash your hands. Next, pour one cup (8 ounces) of warm water into a clean glass. The water should feel warm, not hot. Then add one-half teaspoon of table salt and stir until it dissolves.

To gargle, take a sip of the mixture, tilt your head back, and gargle for about 30 seconds. Spit the water into the sink; do not swallow it. Repeat until the glass is empty. You can gargle several times a day.

Make a fresh mixture each time. Children who are too young to gargle safely should not use this rinse. See a health care provider if your sore throat lasts longer than a week or you have a high fever or trouble breathing.

RP-16.title: Should Community Colleges Offer Free Tutoring Online Around the Clock?
RP-16.text:
Students at community colleges juggle classes with jobs, families, and long commutes. Many of them can only study late at night, long after the campus tutoring center has closed. For these students, free around-the-clock online tutoring is not a luxury; it is the difference between getting help and getting none.

Colleges that have added online tutoring report that the busiest hours are between 9 p.m. and midnight. One college found that students who used online tutoring at least three times in a semester were more likely to pass their math course than students who did not.

Critics argue that online services are expensive. However, the cost of a student failing a course, paying to retake it, and possibly dropping out is far higher, both for the student and for the college. Others worry that online tutors may simply give answers. Good services prevent this by training tutors to ask guiding questions.

If colleges want working adults to succeed, they must offer help when those students are actually able to study.

RP-17.title: How Vaccines Teach the Immune System
RP-17.text:
Your immune system learns from experience. The first time a new germ enters your body, the immune system needs several days to recognize it and build a defense. During that time, you may become sick. Once the infection is over, however, the body keeps special cells called memory cells. If the same germ returns, these cells recognize it quickly, and the body can fight it off before you feel ill.

Vaccines use this ability to learn. A vaccine gives the immune system a safe preview of a germ: a weakened or killed form of it, a harmless piece of it, or instructions that let your own cells make a harmless piece. The immune system responds as if the real germ had arrived and forms memory cells, but you do not get the disease.

Some vaccines need more than one dose, and some, such as the flu vaccine, are updated every year because the virus changes. Like any medicine, vaccines can cause side effects, most often a sore arm or a mild fever for a day or two. Health agencies continue to monitor vaccine safety after vaccines are approved.

RP-18.title: Using a Portable Fire Extinguisher
RP-18.text:
Most portable fire extinguishers work the same way. Before you use one, make sure the fire is small, someone has pulled the fire alarm or called 911, everyone else is leaving the building, and you have a clear exit behind you. If the fire is spreading or the room is filling with smoke, leave immediately and call 911.

To use the extinguisher, remember the word PASS:

P: Pull the pin at the top of the extinguisher. This breaks the seal.
A: Aim the nozzle low, at the base of the fire, not at the flames.
S: Squeeze the handle slowly and evenly.
S: Sweep the nozzle from side to side until the fire appears to be out.

Stand about 6 to 8 feet away from the fire as you begin. Watch the area afterward, because a fire can start again. Even if you put the fire out, report it to the fire department.

RP-20.title: The Storm Shift
RP-20.text:
The power went out at the clinic just after 6 p.m., when the storm was at its worst. For a moment, the waiting room was completely dark. Then the emergency lights flickered on, dim and yellow.

Marcus, the newest medical assistant, felt his heart pound. He had trained for this in a class, but the class had not included rain hammering on the windows or a toddler crying in the corner.

The office manager, Ms. Reyes, didn't raise her voice. She asked Marcus to bring flashlights from the supply closet while she checked that the backup generator had started for the medicine refrigerator. Then she asked him to sit with the patients who were still waiting and explain what was happening. Marcus took a breath, knelt beside the crying toddler's mother, and told her that the doctor would still see them, just by flashlight.

The power came back at 7:40. By then, every patient had been seen. As they locked up, Ms. Reyes said, "Plans help, but people are what get you through." Marcus thought about that all the way home.

RP-21.title: Two Views on Phones in the Classroom
RP-21.text:
Passage A (written by a high school teacher)
Every time a phone buzzes, my students' attention breaks. Even a phone face down on a desk can pull a student's thoughts away from the lesson. Since our school began requiring students to keep phones in their lockers during class, I have seen more discussion, fewer missing assignments, and fewer conflicts that start online and spill into the hallway. Classrooms should be phone-free.

Passage B (written by a parent and emergency medical technician)
I understand why teachers are frustrated, but a total ban goes too far. Phones let families reach students during emergencies, and some students use them to manage health conditions, such as diabetes, with apps. Phones can also be learning tools when teachers plan for them. A better policy would require phones to stay silent and out of sight unless a teacher allows them, with exceptions for medical needs.

RP-24.title: An Accident That Changed Medicine
RP-24.text:
In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation to find that mold had grown on one of the dishes of bacteria he had left in his laboratory. Around the mold was a clear ring where the bacteria had died. Fleming realized that the mold was producing a substance that killed bacteria. He named it penicillin.

Fleming published his findings in 1929, but he could not produce enough pure penicillin to treat patients. For about ten years, little progress was made. Then, around 1940, a team at Oxford University led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain found ways to purify the drug and showed that it could cure infections in mice and then in people.

During World War II, drug companies in the United States worked to produce penicillin in large amounts. By the end of the war, it was saving the lives of many wounded soldiers. In 1945, Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Today, doctors warn that bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics when these drugs are overused or misused. Fleming himself warned about misuse of penicillin in his Nobel lecture.

items.stem: In anatomical position, which term describes the location of the knee relative to the ankle?
items.explanation: Proximal means closer to the point where a limb attaches to the trunk. The knee is closer to the hip than the ankle is, so the knee is proximal to the ankle.

A.text: distal is the reverse (the ankle is distal to the knee).

B.text: medial means toward the midline, which compares side-to-side position, not position along a limb.

D.text: the knee is superior to the ankle, not inferior.

D.text: sagittal planes divide the body into left and right portions (midsagittal into equal halves).

items.stem: Which organs are located in the abdominopelvic cavity? Select all that apply.

C.text: the heart and lungs are in the thoracic cavity, above the diaphragm.

items.stem: Put these structures in the order that inhaled air passes through them.
items.explanation: Air moves from the pharynx (throat) to the larynx (voice box), down the trachea, into the bronchi, through smaller bronchioles, and finally into the alveoli, where gas exchange happens.
generalNotes: Common error: placing the trachea before the larynx. The larynx sits at the top of the trachea, so air passes through it first.

items.stem: Oxygen moves from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillary blood mainly because
items.explanation: Gas exchange in the lungs happens by diffusion. Oxygen moves from where its partial pressure is higher (alveolar air) to where it is lower (blood arriving from the body).

options.text: alveolar cells pump oxygen into the capillary blood.
hemoglobin leaves the capillaries to collect oxygen.
outgoing carbon dioxide pushes oxygen into the blood.
oxygen's partial pressure is higher in alveolar air.

A.text: no active transport is involved; diffusion needs no pumps.

B.text: hemoglobin stays inside red blood cells in the capillaries.

C.text: carbon dioxide diffuses the other way on its own gradient; it does not push oxygen.

items.stem: Which valve keeps blood from flowing backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium?
items.explanation: The mitral valve (also called the bicuspid valve) sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle. It closes when the left ventricle contracts.

A.text: the tricuspid valve is between the right atrium and right ventricle.

C.text: the pulmonary valve is between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk.

D.text: the aortic valve is between the left ventricle and the aorta.

items.stem: Which statement about the pulmonary veins is correct?
items.explanation: Veins are named for direction, not oxygen content: they carry blood toward the heart. The pulmonary veins return freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

options.text: They carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
They carry oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs.
They carry oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium.
They carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the body.

B.text: describes the pulmonary arteries.

C.text: describes the venae cavae.

D.text: describes the aorta. Students who assume every vein carries oxygen-poor blood tend to pick the pulmonary-artery or venae-cavae option.

items.stem: Normally the AV node briefly delays the electrical signal before passing it to the ventricles. If there were no delay, what would most likely happen?
items.explanation: The AV node's delay gives the atria time to finish pushing blood into the ventricles. Without it, the ventricles would contract before they had finished filling, so they would pump less blood with each beat.

options.text: The SA node would stop firing and the heart would stop.
Blood would flow backward through the semilunar valves.
The atria would stop contracting altogether.
The ventricles would contract before they had filled.

A.text: the SA node fires on its own; the AV node does not control it.

B.text: semilunar valves prevent backflow from the arteries regardless of AV timing.

C.text: the atria still receive the signal from the SA node and still contract.

items.stem: Across the walls of which vessels does most exchange of gases and nutrients with body cells take place?
items.explanation: Capillary walls are a single layer of cells, so oxygen, nutrients and wastes can diffuse between blood and tissue. Most exchange happens there.

A.text: arteries and arterioles have thick muscular walls that carry and regulate blood flow.

B.text: arteries and arterioles have thick muscular walls that carry and regulate blood flow.

D.text: vein walls are too thick for meaningful exchange; veins return blood to the heart.

items.stem: Which of the following are formed elements of blood? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: The formed elements are the cells and cell fragments in blood: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

B.text: plasma is the liquid part of blood, not a formed element.

D.text: albumin is a protein dissolved in plasma.

items.stem: Where does most absorption of nutrients into the blood take place?
items.explanation: The small intestine has a huge surface area from circular folds, villi and microvilli. Most digested nutrients are absorbed there.

A.text: the stomach mainly stores and mixes food and begins protein digestion; it absorbs little.

C.text: the large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

D.text: the esophagus only moves food to the stomach.

items.stem: Bile is produced by the liver and stored and concentrated in the ______.
items.explanation: The gallbladder stores bile and concentrates it between meals, then releases it into the small intestine when fatty food arrives.
generalNotes: Common wrong answers: pancreas (makes digestive enzymes, not bile) and liver (makes bile but does not store it).

items.stem: Bile helps the digestion of fats mainly by
items.explanation: Bile emulsifies fat: it breaks large fat globules into many small droplets. This gives the enzyme lipase much more surface to work on. Bile itself contains no digestive enzymes.

options.text: breaking the chemical bonds in fat molecules.
carrying fatty acids directly into the blood.
breaking large fat globules into small droplets.

A.text: chemical digestion of fat is done by lipase, not bile.

B.text: fats are absorbed into intestinal cells and then mostly into lymph, not carried by bile into blood.

C.text: bile enters the small intestine, not the stomach.

items.stem: Which part of a neuron receives signals from other neurons?
items.explanation: Dendrites are branched extensions that receive incoming signals and carry them toward the cell body.

B.text: the axon carries signals away from the cell body.

C.text: axon terminals release neurotransmitter to the next cell.

D.text: myelin insulates the axon and speeds conduction.

items.stem: A person touches a hot pan and jerks the hand away before feeling any pain. This rapid withdrawal is coordinated mainly by the
items.explanation: The withdrawal reflex is routed through the spinal cord: sensory neurons connect through spinal interneurons to motor neurons, so the hand moves without waiting for the brain. The pain signal also travels up to the brain at the same time, which is why the pain is felt a moment after the hand has already moved.

A.text: the cerebrum produces the conscious feeling of pain, which comes after the reflex.

C.text: the cerebellum coordinates smooth, practiced movement.

D.text: the hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger and hormones.

items.stem: Which responses are caused by the sympathetic nervous system? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: The sympathetic division prepares the body for action ('fight or flight'): faster heart rate, wider airways, wider pupils, and more glucose released into the blood for fuel.

options.text: Release of glucose from the liver

A.text: are parasympathetic ('rest and digest') effects: the parasympathetic division increases digestive activity and constricts the pupils.

F.text: are parasympathetic ('rest and digest') effects: the parasympathetic division increases digestive activity and constricts the pupils.

items.stem: Which type of muscle tissue is under voluntary (conscious) control?
items.explanation: Skeletal muscle moves the skeleton and is controlled voluntarily through somatic motor neurons.

A.text: cardiac muscle contracts on its own rhythm.

B.text: smooth muscle in organ and vessel walls is involuntary.

D.text: both are involuntary.

items.stem: During skeletal muscle contraction, sarcomeres shorten because
items.explanation: In the sliding filament model, myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin filaments toward the center. The filaments slide past each other; neither changes length.

options.text: myosin heads pull actin filaments toward the center.
the actin and myosin filaments themselves get shorter.
calcium binds to myosin and makes it longer.
the Z discs at each end of the sarcomere move farther apart.

B.text: the filaments keep their length and only overlap more.

C.text: calcium binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin aside and exposes the binding sites on actin; it does not lengthen myosin.

D.text: the Z discs move closer together as the sarcomere shortens.

items.stem: Where does fertilization of an egg by a sperm normally occur?
items.explanation: Fertilization normally happens in the fallopian (uterine) tube. The early embryo then travels to the uterus and implants in its lining.

A.text: the uterus is where the embryo implants, not where fertilization usually occurs.

B.text: the ovary releases the egg.

C.text: sperm are deposited in the vagina but must travel to the uterine tube.

items.stem: Where are sperm produced?
items.explanation: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules, the coiled tubes inside each testis.

A.text: the epididymis stores sperm while they mature.

C.text: the prostate adds fluid to semen.

D.text: the vas deferens carries sperm toward the urethra.

items.stem: Which layer of the skin has no blood vessels of its own?
items.explanation: The epidermis is avascular. Its living cells get nutrients by diffusion from blood vessels in the dermis below.

A.text: the dermis, including its papillary layer, is well supplied with capillaries.

D.text: the dermis, including its papillary layer, is well supplied with capillaries.

B.text: the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) contains larger blood vessels and fat.

items.stem: On a hot day, how does the skin help lower body temperature?
items.explanation: Dilated dermal vessels bring warm blood close to the surface so heat can leave the body, and evaporating sweat carries more heat away.

options.text: Dermal blood vessels constrict and sweating decreases.
The epidermis thickens to block heat.
Dermal blood vessels dilate and sweating increases.

A.text: this is the response to cold; it conserves heat.

B.text: melanin protects against UV radiation; it does not cool the body.

C.text: the epidermis does not thicken in response to heat.

items.stem: After a large meal, blood glucose rises. Which hormone does the pancreas release in response?
items.explanation: Insulin from pancreatic beta cells lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up glucose and by promoting glycogen storage.

B.text: glucagon is released when blood glucose is low and raises it.

C.text: cortisol (adrenal cortex) raises blood glucose during stress.

D.text: epinephrine (adrenal medulla) also raises blood glucose.

items.stem: Thyroid hormone levels in the blood rise above normal. Which response helps bring them back down?
items.explanation: This is negative feedback. High thyroid hormone inhibits the anterior pituitary (and the hypothalamus), so less thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is released and the thyroid makes less hormone.

options.text: The hypothalamus increases release of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH).
The thyroid gland increases its uptake of iodine from the blood.
The anterior pituitary decreases release of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
The adrenal cortex increases its release of aldosterone into the blood.

A.text: more TRH would push thyroid hormone even higher; in negative feedback, TRH release falls.

B.text: more iodine uptake would support more hormone production, the opposite of what is needed.

D.text: aldosterone regulates sodium and water, not thyroid hormone.

items.stem: Put these structures in the order urine passes through them after it leaves the nephrons.
items.explanation: Urine drains from the collecting ducts through the calyces into the renal pelvis, then down a ureter to the urinary bladder for storage, and leaves the body through the urethra.
generalNotes: Common error: swapping ureter and urethra. The ureters (two) connect kidneys to bladder; the urethra (one) drains the bladder to the outside.

items.stem: What is the effect of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) on the kidneys?
items.explanation: ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water returns to the blood. Urine volume drops and urine becomes more concentrated. 'Antidiuretic' means 'against urine production.'

options.text: Less water is reabsorbed, so urine is more dilute.
More water is reabsorbed, so urine is more concentrated.
More protein is filtered into the urine.
More sodium is excreted in the urine.

A.text: describes low ADH (alcohol, for example, suppresses ADH).

C.text: ADH does not control protein filtration; protein in the urine is a sign of kidney damage.

D.text: ADH acts on water; aldosterone is the main hormone that adjusts sodium.

items.stem: Which cells produce and release antibodies?
items.explanation: When a B cell is activated by its antigen, it divides and many of its descendants become plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of antibody.

A.text: helper T cells coordinate the immune response by signaling other cells but do not make antibodies.

B.text: neutrophils are phagocytes.

C.text: natural killer cells destroy infected or abnormal cells directly.

items.stem: Which of the following are part of the body's innate (nonspecific) defenses? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: Innate defenses work the same way against any invader and do not require earlier exposure to it: physical barriers such as intact skin, and general responses such as fever and inflammation.

A.text: belong to adaptive (specific) immunity, which targets particular antigens. Plasma cells make antibodies during an infection, including a first infection; memory T cells are left behind afterward to respond faster next time.

C.text: belong to adaptive (specific) immunity, which targets particular antigens. Plasma cells make antibodies during an infection, including a first infection; memory T cells are left behind afterward to respond faster next time.

E.text: belong to adaptive (specific) immunity, which targets particular antigens. Plasma cells make antibodies during an infection, including a first infection; memory T cells are left behind afterward to respond faster next time.

items.stem: Which cells break down bone tissue and release calcium into the blood?
items.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb (break down) bone matrix, releasing calcium and phosphate into the blood. Memory aid: osteoClasts Cut bone down; osteoBlasts Build it up.

B.text: osteoblasts build new bone.

C.text: osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain the matrix.

D.text: chondrocytes are cartilage cells.

items.stem: What is the main function of red bone marrow?
items.explanation: Red bone marrow is the site of hematopoiesis: it produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

A.text: yellow marrow stores fat.

B.text: dietary calcium is absorbed in the small intestine.

D.text: cartilage growth happens at growth plates and other cartilage, not in marrow.

items.stem: A swimmer holds her breath underwater. After about a minute, the urge to breathe becomes very strong. Which change in her blood is the main cause of this urge?
items.explanation: Breathing is driven mainly by carbon dioxide. While she holds her breath, CO2 builds up in the blood (making it more acidic), and the brainstem's respiratory centers respond with a strong drive to breathe.

B.text: nitrogen is not used by the body and does not control breathing.

C.text: oxygen falls, not rises, while holding the breath, and in healthy people falling oxygen is a weaker trigger than rising CO2.

D.text: red blood cell count does not change in a minute.

items.stem: During a normal, quiet inhalation, what happens to the diaphragm and to the pressure inside the lungs?
items.explanation: The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves down), enlarging the chest cavity. Larger volume means lower pressure in the lungs, so air flows in from outside where the pressure is higher.

options.text: The diaphragm relaxes and moves up; lung pressure rises.
The diaphragm contracts and moves down; lung pressure falls.
The diaphragm contracts and moves down; lung pressure rises.
The diaphragm relaxes and moves down; lung pressure rises.

A.text: describes quiet exhalation.

C.text: the diaphragm does move down, but a bigger chest cavity lowers lung pressure; higher pressure would push air out.

D.text: a relaxing diaphragm moves up, and rising pressure would push air out.

items.stem: Put these structures in the order food passes through them.
items.explanation: Food moves from the esophagus to the stomach, then through the three parts of the small intestine in order: duodenum, jejunum, ileum.
generalNotes: Common error: putting the ileum before the jejunum. The duodenum is first, the ileum last; it joins the large intestine.

items.stem: Which organ is the main source of the bicarbonate that neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum?
items.explanation: The pancreas sends pancreatic juice, rich in bicarbonate and digestive enzymes, into the duodenum. The bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid so intestinal enzymes can work.

A.text: the liver makes bile, whose main job is emulsifying fat.

B.text: the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; it is not a major source of bicarbonate.

D.text: the large intestine is downstream of the duodenum.

items.stem: After a stroke, a patient has trouble keeping his balance and his movements are jerky and uncoordinated, but his strength is normal. Which brain region was most likely damaged?
items.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance. Damage causes clumsy, poorly coordinated movement even when muscle strength is intact.

A.text: the medulla controls breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

B.text: the occipital lobe processes vision.

C.text: the hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary.

items.stem: Which type of neuron carries signals from the central nervous system out to a muscle?
items.explanation: Motor (efferent) neurons carry signals out of the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands. Memory aid: Efferent Exits.

B.text: sensory (afferent) neurons carry signals in to the CNS.

C.text: interneurons connect neurons within the CNS.

D.text: receptors detect stimuli; they do not carry commands to muscles.

items.stem: A patient's blood calcium level is low. Which hormone will the body release to raise it?
items.explanation: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood calcium. It increases bone breakdown by osteoclasts (indirectly, through other bone cells), increases calcium reabsorption in the kidneys, and activates vitamin D, which increases calcium absorption from food.

A.text: calcitonin lowers blood calcium, the opposite effect.

B.text: insulin lowers blood glucose.

C.text: aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption.

items.stem: During labor, stretching of the cervix triggers the release of oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions that stretch the cervix even more. This is an example of
items.explanation: In positive feedback the response amplifies the original change. Stretching causes oxytocin, which causes more stretching, until delivery ends the loop.

A.text: negative feedback would reduce the stretching and oxytocin release.

B.text: a reflex arc is the nerve pathway from receptor to effector. Nerves do help trigger oxytocin release here, but 'reflex arc' does not describe the self-amplifying loop the question asks about.

D.text: antagonistic hormones (such as insulin and glucagon) have opposite effects on the same variable.

items.stem: A urine test shows glucose in the urine of a patient whose blood glucose is very high. What is the best explanation?
items.explanation: Glucose is normally filtered and then all of it is reabsorbed in the tubules. When blood glucose is very high, more is filtered than the tubules can reabsorb, so the excess spills into the urine.

options.text: The tubules cannot reabsorb all of the filtered glucose.
The glomerulus has stopped filtering glucose.
ADH has increased glucose secretion into the urine.

B.text: if the glomerulus stopped filtering glucose, there would be less glucose in the urine, not more.

C.text: ADH controls water reabsorption, not glucose.

D.text: the bladder only stores urine.

items.stem: A child receives the measles vaccine and is later exposed to measles but does not get sick. Which type of immunity protected the child?
items.explanation: A vaccine is artificial (given on purpose) and the child's own immune system made the antibodies and memory cells, so it is active. Together: artificial active immunity.

A.text: natural active immunity comes from having the disease.

C.text: artificial passive immunity is an injection of ready-made antibodies.

D.text: natural passive immunity is antibodies from the mother, across the placenta or in breast milk.

items.stem: HIV mainly infects and destroys which cells, weakening both antibody and cell-mediated responses?
items.explanation: HIV targets helper T cells (CD4 cells). Because helper T cells activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells, losing them weakens the whole adaptive immune response.

A.text: B cells make antibodies after activation; HIV does not mainly target them, though they lose help from helper T cells.

B.text: cytotoxic (CD8) T cells kill infected cells; they are weakened because they depend on helper T cells, not because HIV infects them.

C.text: neutrophils are innate phagocytes and are not HIV's main target.

items.stem: Which bones are part of the axial skeleton? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: The axial skeleton forms the body's central axis: skull (plus the hyoid and the ear ossicles), vertebral column, ribs and sternum.

A.text: the femur is a limb bone.

D.text: the scapula is part of the shoulder girdle and the hip (coxal) bones form the pelvic girdle; the girdles attach the limbs, so they are appendicular.

F.text: the scapula is part of the shoulder girdle and the hip (coxal) bones form the pelvic girdle; the girdles attach the limbs, so they are appendicular.

items.stem: Which organelle produces most of the ATP a cell uses?
items.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration, which produces most of the cell's ATP.

B.text: ribosomes make proteins.

C.text: the Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins.

D.text: lysosomes digest worn-out parts and debris.

items.stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
items.explanation: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the cell membrane (and chloroplasts and a large central vacuole). Animal cells have no cell wall.

A.text: both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, ribosomes and mitochondria. A common error is thinking plants lack mitochondria because they have chloroplasts.

B.text: both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, ribosomes and mitochondria. A common error is thinking plants lack mitochondria because they have chloroplasts.

D.text: both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, ribosomes and mitochondria. A common error is thinking plants lack mitochondria because they have chloroplasts.

items.stem: A human skin cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have?
items.explanation: Mitosis makes two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same chromosome number as the parent: 46.

options.text: 46 in one cell and 0 in the other

A.text: 23 is the number in gametes made by meiosis.

B.text: 92 is double the parent number. Each chromosome is copied before mitosis, but the copies separate into the two daughter cells, so each gets 46.

D.text: mitosis divides the chromosomes equally between the two cells.

items.stem: Which statements describe meiosis? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: Meiosis produces haploid cells with half the chromosome number (four sperm in males; one egg plus small polar bodies in females), and the cells are genetically different from one another because of crossing over and independent assortment.

options.text: It produces two identical daughter cells.
It is how skin cells replace themselves.

B.text: describe mitosis, which produces two identical body cells for growth and repair.

D.text: describe mitosis, which produces two identical body cells for growth and repair.

items.stem: Put these levels of organization in order from simplest to most complex.
items.explanation: Cells group into tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together as organ systems.
generalNotes: Common error: placing organ before tissue. An organ is made of several tissue types.

items.stem: During transcription, which molecule is made using DNA as a template?
items.explanation: Transcription copies a gene's DNA sequence into messenger RNA in the nucleus. The mRNA then carries the code to a ribosome.

A.text: proteins are made during translation, the next step.

C.text: glucose is not coded by DNA.

D.text: copying DNA into DNA is replication, not transcription.

items.stem: A DNA strand has the sequence A-T-G-C. Which sequence correctly shows the complementary bases, lined up base by base?
items.explanation: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine. So A-T-G-C pairs with T-A-C-G.

A.text: identical, not complementary.

B.text: uracil is found in RNA, not DNA.

C.text: pairs A with C and T with G; the correct pairs are A-T and G-C.

items.stem: Where in the cell does translation (building a protein from mRNA) take place?
items.explanation: Ribosomes read the mRNA codons and link the matching amino acids, brought by tRNA, into a protein.

B.text: the nucleus is where transcription happens.

C.text: lysosomes break molecules down.

D.text: the Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins after ribosomes build them.

items.stem: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white flowers (p). Two plants with genotype Pp are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to have white flowers?
items.explanation: A Punnett square for Pp × Pp gives PP, Pp, Pp and pp. Only pp shows the recessive white color: 1 out of 4.

A.text: white is possible because both parents carry p.

B.text: 1/2 is the fraction that are heterozygous (Pp).

C.text: 3/4 is the fraction with purple flowers.

items.stem: What does the term heterozygous mean?
items.explanation: Heterozygous means the two alleles for a gene are different, such as Pp. Homozygous means they are the same, such as PP or pp.

options.text: Having two identical alleles for a gene
Having two different alleles for a gene

A.text: describes homozygous.

C.text: two recessive alleles is homozygous recessive.

D.text: a heterozygous individual usually shows the dominant trait.

items.stem: A homozygous dominant tall plant (TT) is crossed with a homozygous recessive short plant (tt). What will the offspring be?
items.explanation: Every offspring gets T from one parent and t from the other, so all are Tt. Because T is dominant, all are tall.

B.text: a 1:1 ratio would come from Tt × tt.

C.text: short offspring need tt, which is impossible here.

D.text: TT would require T from both parents.

items.stem: Most enzymes are which type of macromolecule?
items.explanation: Nearly all enzymes are proteins: chains of amino acids folded into a specific shape that speeds up a chemical reaction.

A.text: carbohydrates mainly supply energy and structure.

B.text: lipids store energy and form membranes.

D.text: nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) store and carry genetic information. (A few enzymes are made of RNA, called ribozymes, but most are proteins.)

items.stem: Which type of biomolecule stores the most energy per gram?
items.explanation: Fats (triglycerides, made of glycerol and three fatty acids) store about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates or proteins.

A.text: protein supplies about the same energy per gram as carbohydrate.

B.text: carbohydrate is the body's quickest fuel but stores about half as much energy per gram as fat.

C.text: nucleic acids store genetic information, not energy.

items.stem: What are the building blocks (monomers) of proteins?
items.explanation: Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

A.text: monosaccharides build carbohydrates.

C.text: nucleotides build nucleic acids.

D.text: fatty acids are parts of many lipids.

items.stem: Why are antibiotics NOT effective against the common cold?
items.explanation: Antibiotics act on structures and processes found in bacteria, such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses lack these, so antibiotics do not affect them. Colds are viral.

options.text: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics target bacteria.
Cold-causing bacteria have thick cell walls that block antibiotics from entering.

B.text: colds are not caused by bacteria.

C.text: antibiotics act on bacteria; antifungal drugs treat fungi.

D.text: the immune system does not destroy antibiotics.

items.stem: Which of the following are true of viruses? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: A virus is genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat (capsid). It has no ribosomes or metabolism of its own, so it must use a host cell's machinery to reproduce.

options.text: They can reproduce only inside a host cell.
They enclose their genome in a protein coat (capsid).

A.text: viruses lack ribosomes.

C.text: almost all viruses are much smaller than bacteria.

items.stem: A neutral atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons. What is its mass number?
items.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23. Electrons have almost no mass and are not counted.

A.text: 11 is the atomic number (protons only).

B.text: 22 adds protons and electrons.

D.text: 34 adds all three particles; electrons are not counted in the mass number.

items.stem: Which feature of an atom determines which element it is?
items.explanation: The number of protons is the atomic number, and it defines the element. Every carbon atom has 6 protons; an atom with 7 protons is nitrogen.

A.text: changing neutrons makes a different isotope of the same element.

B.text: gaining or losing electrons makes an ion of the same element.

C.text: energy levels relate to the element's period (row), but the proton count is what defines the element.

items.stem: Sodium and potassium are in the same group (column) of the periodic table. Why do they react in similar ways?
items.explanation: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence (outer-shell) electrons, and valence electrons determine how an element reacts. Sodium and potassium each have one.

options.text: They have the same number of valence electrons.
They have the same atomic mass.
They have the same number of neutrons.
They have the same number of electron energy levels.

B.text: their masses and neutron counts differ (sodium about 23, potassium about 39).

C.text: their masses and neutron counts differ (sodium about 23, potassium about 39).

D.text: elements in the same period (row), not group, have the same number of energy levels.

items.stem: Which of the following is a chemical change?
items.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance (iron oxide) with new properties, so it is a chemical change.

A.text: melting and boiling are changes of state; the substance is still water.

D.text: melting and boiling are changes of state; the substance is still water.

B.text: dissolving is a physical change; evaporating the water gets the sugar back.

items.stem: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) turns directly into a gas without melting. What is this change called?
items.explanation: Sublimation is the change from solid directly to gas.

B.text: deposition is the reverse, gas directly to solid (frost).

C.text: condensation is gas to liquid.

D.text: evaporation is liquid to gas.

items.stem: Which of the following are physical changes? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: In a physical change the substance keeps its identity: cut paper is still paper, melted butter is still butter, and dissolved sugar is still sugar (evaporate the water and it is left behind).

B.text: are chemical changes: burning and baking form new substances (ash, gases, new compounds in the cake).

D.text: are chemical changes: burning and baking form new substances (ash, gases, new compounds in the cake).

items.stem: Which set of coefficients balances this equation? __ H₂ + __ O₂ → __ H₂O
items.explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Left: 4 H and 2 O. Right: 4 H and 2 O. Atoms are conserved.

A.text: 2 O on the left but only 1 on the right.

C.text: 4 O on the left, 1 on the right.

D.text: 4 O on the left, 2 on the right.

items.stem: What type of reaction is Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂?
items.explanation: One element (zinc) replaces another (hydrogen) in a compound: A + BC → AC + B. That is single replacement.

A.text: synthesis combines substances into one product (A + B → AB).

B.text: decomposition breaks one compound apart (AB → A + B).

C.text: combustion is a reaction with oxygen that releases energy, usually making CO₂ and water.

items.stem: In a sealed container, 10 grams of reactants react completely. What is the total mass of the products?
items.explanation: The law of conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so the products have the same mass as the reactants in a closed system.

options.text: Less than 10 grams, because some mass becomes energy
More than 10 grams, because new bonds add mass
It cannot be predicted without the balanced equation

A.text: in ordinary chemical reactions the mass change is far too small to measure.

C.text: forming bonds does not add atoms.

D.text: conservation of mass holds for every chemical reaction, so no equation is needed.

items.stem: Which change would NOT speed up a chemical reaction?
items.explanation: Removing a catalyst slows the reaction, because the catalyst was lowering the activation energy.

options.text: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
Grinding a solid reactant into powder

A.text: higher temperature makes particles move faster and collide harder and more often.

B.text: higher concentration means more frequent collisions.

C.text: powder has more surface area, so more particles are exposed to collide.

items.stem: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
items.explanation: A catalyst provides an easier pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed. It is not consumed.

options.text: It lowers the activation energy needed.
It raises the temperature of the mixture.
It is used up to supply extra energy.
It increases the total amount of product made.

B.text: catalysts do not heat the mixture.

C.text: catalysts are not used up.

D.text: a catalyst makes product faster but does not change how much product the reaction can make.

items.stem: Why does food spoil more slowly in a refrigerator?
items.explanation: Spoilage involves chemical reactions, many driven by microbes' enzymes. At lower temperature particles move more slowly and collide less often and with less energy, so the reactions slow down.

options.text: Cold makes food molecules more stable by adding energy to them.
Cold temperatures kill the bacteria and molds that make food spoil.
Particles move less at lower temperature, so reaction rates drop.
The refrigerator removes moisture, which spoilage reactions need.

A.text: cooling removes energy; it does not add it.

B.text: refrigeration slows the growth of most bacteria and molds but does not kill them.

D.text: refrigerators do not dry food out enough to matter, and reactions still occur, just more slowly.

items.stem: In salt water, what is the salt?
items.explanation: The solute is the substance that is dissolved (salt). The solvent does the dissolving (water). Together they make the solution.

A.text: water is the solvent.

C.text: the solution is the whole mixture.

D.text: a precipitate is a solid that comes out of a solution.

items.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic solution (one with a higher solute concentration than the cell). What happens to the cell?
items.explanation: Water moves by osmosis toward the higher solute concentration. The solution outside is more concentrated, so water leaves the cell and it shrinks (crenates).

options.text: It takes in salt from the solution and swells.
It shrinks as water leaves it.

A.text: swelling happens in a hypotonic solution, where water moves in.

B.text: no change happens in an isotonic solution.

C.text: water moves, not salt, and the cell loses water.

items.stem: How many grams of glucose are in 250 mL of a 5% (weight/volume) glucose solution? Enter a number.
items.explanation: A 5% (w/v) solution has 5 g per 100 mL. 250 mL is 2.5 × 100 mL, so 2.5 × 5 g = 12.5 g.
generalNotes: Common errors: 5 × 250 = 1,250 (forgetting that percent means per 100 mL); 50 (treating 5% as per 25 mL).

items.stem: A solution has a pH of 3. Which statement best describes it?
items.explanation: Below pH 7 is acidic, and a lower pH means more hydrogen ions. pH 3 has 10,000 times the H⁺ concentration of pure water (pH 7).

options.text: It is acidic, with more H⁺ ions than pure water.
It is basic, with more OH⁻ ions than pure water.
It is neutral, like pure water.
It is acidic, with fewer H⁺ ions than pure water.

B.text: basic solutions have pH above 7.

C.text: neutral is pH 7.

D.text: acidic is right, but acids have more H⁺ than water, not fewer; this reverses the scale.

items.stem: A solution at pH 4 has how many times the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution at pH 6?
items.explanation: Each pH unit is a tenfold change. Two units apart: 10 × 10 = 100 times. Lower pH means more hydrogen ions.

A.text: subtracts the pH values (6 − 4) instead of using powers of 10.

B.text: multiplies 2 by 10.

D.text: would be three pH units apart.

items.stem: When an acid reacts completely with a base, what are the usual products?
items.explanation: This is a neutralization reaction: acid + base → salt + water. For example, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

B.text: hydrogen gas comes from an acid reacting with certain metals.

C.text: neutralization weakens the acid.

D.text: carbon dioxide comes from combustion or from an acid reacting with a carbonate.

items.stem: A nurse needs to measure exactly 37 mL of a liquid. Which of these tools gives the most precise measurement?
items.explanation: A graduated cylinder is narrow and finely marked, so it measures liquid volume much more precisely than the other choices.

A.text: beakers and flasks have rough markings meant only for estimates.

B.text: beakers and flasks have rough markings meant only for estimates.

D.text: most test tubes have no volume markings.

items.stem: Convert 2.5 kilograms to grams. Enter a number.
items.explanation: Kilo- means 1,000, so 1 kg = 1,000 g. 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500 g. Moving to a smaller unit gives a bigger number.
generalNotes: Common errors: 250 (multiplying by 100); 0.0025 (dividing instead of multiplying).

items.stem: Water in a graduated cylinder has a curved surface (a meniscus). How should you read the volume?
items.explanation: Water curves down in the middle, forming a meniscus. Read the bottom of the meniscus with your eye level with it to avoid parallax error.

options.text: At the top edge of the curved surface, looking down from above
At the bottom of the curve, with your eye level with it
At the highest marking on the cylinder that the water touches along the glass
At the average of the top and bottom of the curve

A.text: reading the edge overestimates the volume, and looking from above adds parallax error.

C.text: water clings up the glass at the edges, so this overestimates.

D.text: there is no averaging rule; read the bottom of the curve with your eye level with it.

items.stem: Which statement about a patient is an inference rather than an observation?
items.explanation: An inference is a conclusion drawn from observations. "Probably has an infection" interprets the data; the other statements report what was measured or seen.

options.text: The patient's skin is red and warm.
The patient probably has an infection.
The patient's heart rate is 110 beats per minute.

A.text: each is an observation gathered directly by measurement or the senses.

B.text: each is an observation gathered directly by measurement or the senses.

D.text: each is an observation gathered directly by measurement or the senses.

items.stem: Which evidence would best support the claim that Drug X lowers blood pressure?
items.explanation: A large randomized trial with a placebo control group directly measures blood pressure and compares it fairly, so it is the strongest evidence.

options.text: A well-known athlete says Drug X lowered her own blood pressure.
Ten people who already take Drug X say on a survey that they now feel much healthier.
An advertisement from the drug's maker says it is the best treatment.
In a large randomized trial, Drug X lowered pressure more than a placebo did.

A.text: a single testimonial is anecdotal.

B.text: a small, self-selected group reporting feelings, not measured blood pressure.

C.text: the maker has a conflict of interest and gives no data.

items.stem: A study finds that towns with more hospitals also have more deaths each year. What is the best conclusion?
items.explanation: Correlation does not show causation. Larger towns have both more hospitals and more deaths simply because more people live there.

options.text: Hospitals cause more people to die, so towns should build fewer of them.
More deaths cause towns to build more hospitals to keep up with demand.
The data must contain an error, because hospitals are known to save lives.
They are correlated; a third factor, such as population, may explain both.

A.text: each assumes one causes the other without evidence.

B.text: each assumes one causes the other without evidence.

C.text: the pattern is real and expected, so there is no reason to assume an error.

items.stem: A student measures an enzyme's activity. Activity rises steadily from 20 °C to 40 °C, then drops sharply between 40 °C and 50 °C. What is the best prediction for its activity at 60 °C?
items.explanation: The data show a peak near 40 °C and a sharp drop above it, the pattern of an enzyme denaturing. Extending the trend, activity at 60 °C should be very low.

options.text: Very low, because high heat changes the enzyme's shape
Higher than at 40 °C, because heat speeds up reactions
About the same as at 20 °C, because the curve repeats
Twice the activity at 40 °C, because the temperature is higher

B.text: ignores the drop above 40 °C.

C.text: nothing in the data suggests the curve repeats.

D.text: assumes a straight-line relationship the data contradict.

items.stem: A sealed syringe of air is kept at constant temperature. If you push the plunger in so the volume of air decreases, what happens to the pressure of the air?
items.explanation: Pressure and volume of a gas are inversely related at constant temperature (Boyle's law): the same particles in less space hit the walls more often, so pressure rises.

A.text: describes a direct relationship, which is wrong for pressure and volume.

B.text: the change in volume does change pressure.

D.text: pressure would drop only if the gas were removed.

items.stem: A student records the boiling point of water at different altitudes: sea level, 100 °C; 1,500 m, 95 °C; 3,000 m, 90 °C. Assuming the pattern continues, what is the best prediction for the boiling point at 4,500 m?
items.explanation: The boiling point drops about 5 °C for every 1,500 m of altitude. One more 1,500 m step below 90 °C gives 85 °C.

A.text: drops 10 °C, twice the observed step.

C.text: assumes the boiling point stops changing.

D.text: reverses the trend.

items.stem: A student tests how fertilizer affects plant growth. She gives four groups of plants 0, 5, 10 and 15 grams of fertilizer and measures their height after three weeks. What is the independent variable?
items.explanation: The independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes: the amount of fertilizer.

B.text: plant height is the dependent variable, the result being measured.

C.text: these should be kept the same for all groups (controlled variables).

D.text: these should be kept the same for all groups (controlled variables).

items.stem: A student gives four groups of plants 0, 5, 10 and 15 grams of fertilizer and measures their height after three weeks. What is the purpose of the group that receives 0 grams?
items.explanation: The 0-gram group is the control: it shows how plants grow without the treatment, so the effect of fertilizer can be measured against it.

options.text: It is the control, used for comparison.
It shows the best amount of fertilizer.
It proves that the hypothesis is correct.

A.text: the dependent variable is plant height, a measurement, not a group.

C.text: the 0-gram group alone cannot show the best amount; that requires comparing results across all the groups.

D.text: experiments support or refute a hypothesis; they do not prove it.

items.stem: Put these steps of the scientific method in the usual order.
items.explanation: Observe and ask a question, form a testable hypothesis, test it with an experiment, analyze the data, then draw a conclusion about whether the data support the hypothesis.

options.text: Make an observation and ask a question

generalNotes: Common error: placing the hypothesis after the experiment. The hypothesis is the prediction the experiment tests.

items.stem: Which statement is a testable hypothesis?
items.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction, often in if-then form, that an experiment can support or refute.

options.text: Plants are the most beautiful living things.
If plants get more light, they will grow taller.
The plant grew 5 centimeters last week.
Gardeners should water their plants in the morning.

A.text: an opinion cannot be tested.

C.text: an observation (a measurement already made).

D.text: a recommendation, not a prediction an experiment could support or refute.

items.stem: Which decimal is equal to 3/8?
items.explanation: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.

B.text: 0.38 is 0.375 rounded, not equal.

C.text: reverses the digits.

D.text: misplaces the decimal point (that is 3/80).

items.stem: Write 0.045 as a percent. Enter a number.
items.explanation: To change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100 (move the decimal point two places right): 0.045 → 4.5%.
generalNotes: Common errors: 45% (moving three places); 0.45% (moving one place).

items.stem: What is 2/3 + 1/4?
items.explanation: Use a common denominator of 12: 2/3 = 8/12 and 1/4 = 3/12. 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

A.text: adds numerators and denominators straight across.

C.text: multiplies the fractions instead of adding.

D.text: correct numerator, but doubles the common denominator.

items.explanation: A negative times a negative is positive: (−8) × (−3) = 24. Then 24 ÷ 4 = 6.

A.text: forgets to divide by 4.

B.text: give the product the wrong sign; two negatives make a positive.

C.text: give the product the wrong sign; two negatives make a positive.

items.stem: Put these numbers in order from least to greatest.
items.explanation: Convert everything to decimals: 0.6, 5/8 = 0.625, 58% = 0.58, 0.65. In order: 0.58, 0.6, 0.625, 0.65.
generalNotes: Common error: treating 5/8 as 0.58 or 58% as 5.8.

items.stem: Which of these values is the greatest?
items.explanation: As decimals: 0.09, 1/9 ≈ 0.111, 11% = 0.11, and 0.1. The greatest is 1/9 (0.111 is a little more than 0.110).

A.text: 0.09 is the smallest.

C.text: 11% = 0.110, just less than 0.111.

D.text: 0.1 is less than 0.111.

items.stem: Solve for x: 3x − 7 = 11
items.explanation: Add 7 to both sides: 3x = 18. Divide both sides by 3: x = 6. Check: 3(6) − 7 = 11.

A.text: subtracts 7 instead of adding it (3x = 4).

B.text: stops before dividing by 3.

D.text: ignores the −7 (3x = 11).

items.stem: Solve for x: 5(x + 2) = 35. Enter a number.
items.explanation: Divide both sides by 5: x + 2 = 7. Subtract 2: x = 5. Check: 5(5 + 2) = 35.
generalNotes: Common errors: 6.6 (distributing as 5x + 2 = 35); 7 (forgetting to subtract 2).

items.stem: A patient drinks 240 mL at breakfast, 180 mL mid-morning and 350 mL at lunch. What is the patient's total fluid intake?

A.text: addition errors; line up the place values and add carefully.

B.text: addition errors; line up the place values and add carefully.

D.text: addition errors; line up the place values and add carefully.

items.stem: A nurse works three 12-hour shifts each week and earns $32.50 per hour. What is the nurse's weekly pay before taxes?

C.text: rounds the rate up to $33.

D.text: pays for only one 12-hour shift.

items.stem: A $60 textbook is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price?

A.text: the discount, not the price.

B.text: subtracts $25 instead of 25%.

D.text: takes 20% off instead of 25%.

items.stem: A patient's weight drops from 80 kg to 72 kg. What is the percent decrease?
items.explanation: Percent change = change ÷ original × 100. The change is 8 kg; 8 ÷ 80 = 0.10 = 10%.

A.text: divides by the new weight (8 ÷ 72).

B.text: gives the change in kilograms, not percent.

C.text: the new weight as a percent of the original.

items.stem: A calculated medication volume is 3.4762 mL. The syringe is marked in hundredths of a milliliter. Round the volume to the nearest hundredth.
items.explanation: The hundredths digit is 7. The next digit, 6, is 5 or more, so round up: 3.48 mL.

B.text: truncates instead of rounding.

C.text: rounds to the nearest tenth.

D.text: rounds to the nearest thousandth.

items.stem: A student buys 12.2 gallons of gas at $3.89 per gallon. By first rounding each number to the nearest whole number, estimate the cost.
items.explanation: 12.2 rounds to 12 and $3.89 rounds to $4. 12 × $4 = $48. (The exact cost is about $47.46.)

A.text: drops the decimals instead of rounding (12 × 3).

C.text: rounds both numbers up (13 × 4).

D.text: rounds 12.2 to 10.

items.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour to make 24 cookies. How many cups of flour are needed to make 40 cookies?
items.explanation: Set up the proportion 3/24 = x/40. Cross-multiply: 24x = 120, so x = 5 cups.

A.text: doubles the flour.

B.text: adds 1 cup without setting up the proportion.

C.text: 24 ÷ 3, the number of cookies per cup, not the cups needed.

items.stem: A liquid medication contains 250 mg in 5 mL. How many mL contain 400 mg? Enter a number.
items.explanation: Set up 250 mg / 5 mL = 400 mg / x mL. Cross-multiply: 250x = 2,000, so x = 8 mL.
generalNotes: Common errors: 3.125 (inverting the ratio); 80 (misplacing the decimal).

items.stem: A class has 12 men and 18 women. What is the ratio of men to women in simplest form?
items.explanation: 12:18 divided by the greatest common factor, 6, gives 2:3.

B.text: women to men.

C.text: men to the whole class, not simplified.

D.text: men to the whole class.

items.stem: A car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed?
items.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 miles per hour.

A.text: multiplies instead of dividing.

B.text: ignores the half hour (150 ÷ 2).

D.text: rounds 2.5 hours up to 3 (150 ÷ 3).

items.stem: A gym charges a $50 sign-up fee plus $25 per month. Which expression gives the total cost for m months?
items.explanation: The $50 fee is paid once; $25 is paid each month, so 25m. Total: 50 + 25m.

B.text: swaps the one-time and monthly amounts.

C.text: charges the sign-up fee every month.

D.text: leaves out the one-time $50 sign-up fee.

items.stem: Maria needs at least $600 for tuition. She has saved $150 and earns $15 per hour. Which inequality can be used to find the number of hours, h, she must work?
items.explanation: Her total is what she has plus what she earns: 150 + 15h. "At least $600" means greater than or equal to, so 150 + 15h ≥ 600.

A.text: "at most," the wrong direction.

B.text: swaps the savings and the hourly pay.

C.text: swaps the amounts and uses the wrong direction.

items.stem:
A patient's temperature was recorded each morning:

Day | Temperature
Monday | 98.6 °F
Tuesday | 99.1 °F
Wednesday | 100.4 °F
Thursday | 99.5 °F
Friday | 98.8 °F

By how much did the temperature rise from Monday to its highest reading?
items.explanation: The highest reading is Wednesday, 100.4 °F. 100.4 − 98.6 = 1.8 °F.

A.text: Monday to Tuesday only.

B.text: 100 − 98.6, dropping the 0.4.

D.text: in the tenths column, subtracts the smaller digit from the larger (6 − 4 = 2) instead of borrowing, then 100 − 98 = 2, giving 2.2.

items.stem:
A clinic recorded these monthly visits:

Month | Visits
January | 120
February | 150
March | 140
April | 180

Between which two consecutive months did visits increase the most?
items.explanation: Changes: January to February +30, February to March −10, March to April +40. The largest increase between consecutive months is March to April.

A.text: an increase of 30, less than 40.

B.text: visits went down.

D.text: January and April are not consecutive months.

items.stem: What is the mean of this data set: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13?
items.explanation: Add the values: 4 + 7 + 7 + 9 + 13 = 40. Divide by the number of values, 5: 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

A.text: the median and the mode.

B.text: the range (13 − 4).

D.text: the sum, not divided by 5.

items.stem: For the data set 3, 5, 5, 8, 9, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: Median: the middle value of the ordered list is 5. Range: 9 − 3 = 6. Mode: 5 (it appears twice). Mean: 30 ÷ 5 = 6.

B.text: the mode is the most frequent value, 5.

D.text: the mean is 6; 5 is the median and the mode.

items.stem: A study finds that as the number of hours students study increases, their test scores also increase. Which describes this relationship?
items.explanation: When two variables increase together, they have a positive correlation.

A.text: in a negative (inverse) relationship, one goes up as the other goes down.

D.text: in a negative (inverse) relationship, one goes up as the other goes down.

C.text: the variables clearly change together.

items.stem: In the equation y = 4x + 3, how does y change when x increases by 2?
items.explanation: The slope, 4, means y increases by 4 for every 1-unit increase in x. For an increase of 2: 4 × 2 = 8.

B.text: assumes y changes by the same amount as x.

C.text: adds the 3, which is the starting value, not part of the change.

D.text: the change for an increase of 1, not 2.

items.stem: A rectangular room is 12 feet wide and 15 feet long. What is its area?
items.explanation: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 15 × 12 = 180 square feet.

A.text: the perimeter (2 × 12 + 2 × 15), in the wrong units.

C.text: adds the sides.

D.text: doubles the area.

items.stem: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. What is its circumference? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.explanation: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 cm.

A.text: uses πr (forgets the 2).

B.text: the area, πr².

C.text: squares the radius.

items.stem: A patient weighs 165 pounds. What is the patient's weight in kilograms? (1 kg = 2.2 lb)
items.explanation: Kilograms are heavier than pounds, so the number gets smaller: 165 ÷ 2.2 = 75 kg.

B.text: multiplies instead of dividing.

C.text: divides by 2.

D.text: a division error.

items.stem: How many milliliters are in 8 fluid ounces? (1 fl oz ≈ 30 mL) Enter a number.
generalNotes: Common error: dividing (8 ÷ 30) instead of multiplying.

items.stem: A patient has taken 3/5 of a prescribed course of antibiotics. What percent of the course is left?

A.text: the part already taken.

B.text: forgets to multiply 0.4 by 100.

D.text: moves the decimal point only one place.

items.stem: Which of these are equal to 3/4? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 = 75%. 6/8 simplifies to 3/4 (divide top and bottom by 2).

C.text: writes the digits of the fraction as a decimal.

D.text: moves the decimal point only one place (0.075).

items.stem: A recipe calls for 2 1/2 cups of flour. How many cups are needed to make 1 1/2 batches?
items.explanation: Convert to improper fractions: 5/2 × 3/2 = 15/4 = 3 3/4 cups.

A.text: adds instead of multiplying (2 1/2 + 1 1/2).

B.text: multiplies the whole numbers and the fractions separately (2 × 1 + 1/2 × 1/2).

C.text: divides instead of multiplying.

items.stem: Evaluate: 18 − 4 × (5 − 2)² ÷ 6. Enter a number.
items.explanation: Parentheses: 5 − 2 = 3. Exponent: 3² = 9. Multiply and divide left to right: 4 × 9 = 36, 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Subtract: 18 − 6 = 12.
generalNotes: Common errors: 21 (working left to right without the order of operations: 18 − 4 = 14, 14 × 9 = 126, 126 ÷ 6 = 21); 4 (squaring each number before subtracting: 5² − 2² = 21, then 4 × 21 ÷ 6 = 14, 18 − 14 = 4).

items.stem: Which list is in order from least to greatest?
items.explanation: As decimals: −0.6, −0.5, 0.05, 0.25. The negative farther from zero (−0.6) is smallest.

A.text: treats −0.6 as greater than −0.5.

C.text: treats 0.05 as greater than 0.25.

D.text: ignores the negative signs.

items.stem: Four students reported their quiz results: Ana 5/6, Ben 0.81, Cal 82%, Dee 4/5. Who scored the highest?
items.explanation: As decimals: Ana 0.833…, Ben 0.81, Cal 0.82, Dee 0.80. Ana's 5/6 is the greatest.

B.text: rounds 5/6 down to 0.8 and moves 82% the wrong way (0.082), so 0.81 looks largest.

C.text: compares the numbers as written; 82 looks biggest.

D.text: reasons that fifths are bigger pieces than sixths, so 4/5 must beat 5/6; in fact 4/5 = 0.80 < 0.833.

items.stem: Solve for x: 2(3x − 4) = 4x + 10
items.explanation: Distribute: 6x − 8 = 4x + 10. Subtract 4x: 2x − 8 = 10. Add 8: 2x = 18. Divide by 2: x = 9.

A.text: distributes only to the first term (6x − 4 = 4x + 10).

B.text: subtracts 8 instead of adding it (2x = 2).

D.text: stops before dividing by 2.

items.stem: Solve for x: x/3 − 4 = 2. Enter a number.
items.explanation: Add 4 to both sides: x/3 = 6. Multiply both sides by 3: x = 18.
generalNotes: Common errors: 2 (dividing 6 by 3 instead of multiplying); −6 (subtracting 4 instead of adding).

items.stem: An IV of 1,500 mL is ordered to run over 12 hours. After 5 hours, only 500 mL has been infused. To the nearest whole number, at what rate in mL per hour must the rest run to finish on time?
items.explanation: Remaining volume: 1,500 − 500 = 1,000 mL. Remaining time: 12 − 5 = 7 hours. 1,000 ÷ 7 ≈ 142.9, about 143 mL/hr.

A.text: the original rate (1,500 ÷ 12).

C.text: divides the remaining volume by the hours already used (1,000 ÷ 5).

D.text: the rate so far (500 ÷ 5).

items.stem: Store A sells 3 pounds of apples for $7.47. Store B sells 5 pounds for $11.95. How much do you save per pound by buying at Store B?
items.explanation: Store A: $7.47 ÷ 3 = $2.49 per pound. Store B: $11.95 ÷ 5 = $2.39 per pound. Savings: $2.49 − $2.39 = $0.10 per pound.

B.text: Store B's price per pound, not the savings.

C.text: the difference in total prices, which compares different amounts.

D.text: Store A's price per pound.

items.stem: A store marks up an $80 item by 25%. Later it puts the item on sale at 30% off the marked-up price. What is the sale price?

A.text: combines the percents first (25% − 30% = −5%) and takes 5% off $80.

C.text: the marked-up price before the sale.

D.text: takes 30% off the original $80 and ignores the markup.

items.stem: A town's population grew from 2,400 to 2,700. What was the percent increase? Enter the percent as a number (for example, 12.5).
generalNotes: Common errors: 11.1 (dividing by the new value, 300 ÷ 2,700); 300 (the increase, not a percent).

items.stem: A family's weekly grocery bills were $187.42, $203.15, $194.88 and $212.67. Estimate the four-week total by first rounding each bill to the nearest ten dollars.
items.explanation: Rounded to the nearest $10: $190, $200, $190 and $210. Sum: $790. (The exact total is $798.12.)

B.text: rounds each bill to the nearest hundred dollars.

C.text: drops the ones digit instead of rounding ($180, $200, $190, $210).

D.text: rounds every bill up to the next ten.

items.stem: A clinic saw 612 patients last month, and 48% of them were over age 50. Which is the best estimate of the number of patients over age 50?
items.explanation: 48% is close to 50% (one half), and 612 is close to 600. Half of 600 is 300. (The exact value is 293.76, about 294 patients.)

A.text: misplace the decimal point.

C.text: misplace the decimal point.

B.text: ignores the 0.48 and keeps only 612 rounded.

items.stem: On a map, 1 cm represents 2.5 km. Two towns are 18.5 km apart. How far apart are they on the map?
items.explanation: Set up 1 cm / 2.5 km = x cm / 18.5 km. Cross-multiply: 2.5x = 18.5, so x = 7.4 cm.

A.text: multiplies instead of dividing (18.5 × 2.5).

B.text: subtracts (18.5 − 2.5).

C.text: misplaces the decimal point.

items.stem: A child weighs 44 lb. A medication is ordered at 15 mg per kg of body weight. How many milligrams should the child receive? (1 kg = 2.2 lb) Enter a number.
items.explanation: Convert weight: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. Dose: 20 kg × 15 mg/kg = 300 mg.
generalNotes: Common errors: 660 (using pounds as kilograms: 44 × 15); 1,452 (multiplying by 2.2 instead of dividing).

items.stem: A cleaning solution mixes concentrate and water in a ratio of 2:7. How much concentrate is needed to make 1,350 mL of solution?
items.explanation: The ratio has 2 + 7 = 9 parts. One part = 1,350 ÷ 9 = 150 mL. Concentrate is 2 parts: 300 mL.

B.text: uses 2/7 of the total instead of 2/9.

C.text: one part only.

D.text: the amount of water (7 parts).

items.stem: A runner finishes a 10-kilometer race in 50 minutes. What is her average speed in kilometers per hour?
items.explanation: 50 minutes = 50/60 hour. Speed = 10 ÷ (50/60) = 10 × 60/50 = 12 km per hour.

A.text: the speed in kilometers per minute (10 ÷ 50).

B.text: divides 50 by 10.

D.text: divides 10 by 0.5, treating 50 minutes as half an hour.

items.stem: A plumber charges a $50 service fee plus $25 per hour. A customer's bill is $200. How many hours did the plumber work?
items.explanation: Set up 50 + 25h = 200. Subtract 50: 25h = 150. Divide by 25: h = 6 hours.

A.text: divides the whole bill by the hourly rate (200 ÷ 25) and ignores the fee.

C.text: adds the fee instead of subtracting it ((200 + 50) ÷ 25).

D.text: divides the remaining $150 by the $50 fee instead of the hourly rate.

items.stem: A phone's battery is at 85% and drops 4% for each hour of video. The inequality 85 − 4h > 20 describes keeping the battery above 20%. Which numbers of hours, h, satisfy the inequality? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: Subtract 85: −4h > −65. Divide by −4 and flip the sign: h < 16.25. Of the choices, 10, 16 and 15 are less than 16.25.

C.text: forgetting to flip the sign gives h > 16.25, which would wrongly select 17 and 20.

D.text: forgetting to flip the sign gives h > 16.25, which would wrongly select 17 and 20.

items.stem:
A hospital unit's yearly budget of $350,000 is divided as follows:

Category | Share of budget
Staff | 62%
Supplies | 18%
Equipment | 12%
Other | 8%

How much more is budgeted for supplies than for equipment?

A.text: the supplies budget alone.

B.text: the equipment budget alone.

C.text: treats the 6% difference as $6,000.

items.stem:
