A.text: "I" can't follow "to"; test: "gave the handouts to I."

B.text: after the preposition "between," use "me."

D.text: the subject needs "He"; test: "Him finished early."

items.stem: Which sentence uses fewer or less correctly?
items.explanation: Use "fewer" for things you can count and "less" for amounts.

options.text: There were less patients in the clinic today.
We need fewer water for this recipe.
She drank fewer coffee this week.
There were fewer patients in the clinic today.

A.text: patients can be counted, so use "fewer."

B.text: water is an amount, not a count, so use "less."

C.text: coffee is an amount, so use "less."

items.stem: Which sentence is written in the active voice?
items.explanation: In the active voice the subject (the technician) does the action.

options.text: The samples were collected by the technician.
The samples had been collected before noon.
Mistakes were made during the procedure.

B.text: passive: the subject (samples) receives the action.

C.text: passive, and the doer isn't named.

D.text: passive, and the doer isn't named.

items.stem:
Which revision of this sentence is clearest and most concise?

Due to the fact that the road was closed, we were late.
items.explanation: "Because" replaces the five-word phrase "due to the fact that" without losing meaning.

options.text: Because the road was closed, we were late.
Due to the fact of the road closure, we were late.
Owing to the fact that the road was closed, we were late.
Due to the fact that there was a road closure, we were late.

B.text: keeps the wordy "due to the fact."

C.text: just as wordy as the original.

D.text: even wordier than the original.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an adjective or adverb correctly?
items.explanation: "Correctly" is an adverb describing the action verb "answered."

options.text: He did really good on the exam.

A.text: "sings" is an action verb, so it needs the adverb "well."

B.text: "smells" is a linking verb here, so it needs the adjective "good."

C.text: "did" is an action verb, so it needs "well."

items.stem:
Which verb correctly completes the sentence?

There ___ several reasons to arrive early.
items.explanation: In a "There is/There are" sentence, the subject comes after the verb. "Reasons" is plural, so use "are."

A.text: the subject comes after the verb: "reasons" is plural.

C.text: singular; the subject "reasons" is plural.

D.text: singular; the subject "reasons" is plural.

items.stem: Which sentence avoids an unclear pronoun reference?
items.explanation: Repeating the name removes any doubt about who was at work.

options.text: The doctor told the nurse that she needed a break.
When Sam called Raj, Sam was still at work.
When the cup hit the tray, it broke.
They say the clinic is closing.

A.text: "she" could mean the doctor or the nurse.

C.text: "it" could mean the cup or the tray.

D.text: "They" doesn't refer to anyone named.

items.stem: Which sentence is most appropriate for a cover letter for a nursing assistant job?
items.explanation: A cover letter calls for a polite, formal, and specific tone.

options.text: I am excited to apply for your nursing assistant position.
I'm super pumped to work at your totally awesome hospital this year!
Hire me for this job right away. You definitely won't regret it.
I really need this job badly because my bills keep piling up.

B.text: slang and exaggeration are too informal for a cover letter.

C.text: a pushy command that's too demanding for a cover letter.

D.text: informal, and it focuses on the writer's need, not what they offer.

items.stem: A writer wants to describe a patient's attitude in a positive way. Which word fits best?
items.explanation: All four words describe someone who won't give up or give in, but only "determined" has a positive connotation.

A.text: similar meaning but a negative connotation.

B.text: similar meaning but a negative connotation.

D.text: negative and informal.

items.stem: Which sentence is most appropriate for a lab report?
items.explanation: A lab report should be objective and precise, reporting measured results.

options.text: We think the plants probably grew more because of the light, maybe.
The plants kept in light grew 4 cm more than the plants kept in the dark.
The light made the plants grow like crazy compared to the dark ones.
I was totally amazed by how much the plants in the light grew!

A.text: vague and full of hedging words.

C.text: slang, and gives no measurement.

D.text: emotional, and gives no data.

items.stem: A pamphlet is titled "Why You Should Get a Flu Shot." What is the main purpose of the pamphlet?
items.explanation: "Why you should" signals an argument meant to convince the reader to act.

options.text: To entertain readers with a story
To explain how the flu virus was discovered
To persuade readers to get vaccinated

A.text: the title gives reasons, not a story.

B.text: the title isn't about history.

C.text: the topic is the flu shot, not a nurse's day.

items.stem: A nurse is writing discharge instructions for a patient. Which sentence is best?
items.explanation: Patient instructions should use plain, specific language.

options.text: Ambulate TID and maintain NPO status after midnight before your procedure.
Try to get some walking in and maybe skip eating late at night.
Walk three times a day, and don't eat or drink anything after midnight.
Ambulation and NPO adherence after midnight are recommended for you.

A.text: medical abbreviations the patient may not understand.

B.text: too vague: how often, and what exactly to skip?

D.text: jargon the patient may not understand, and it doesn't say how often to walk.

items.stem: Which phrase uses person-first language?
items.explanation: Person-first language names the person first and the condition second.

options.text: the patient with diabetes in room 4

B.text: puts the condition before the person.

C.text: calls the person a "case."

D.text: puts the condition before the person.

items.stem: Which message is the most appropriate text to a close friend?
items.explanation: Informal, short messages suit a close friend. The best register depends on the audience.

options.text: Dear Ms. Lopez, I regret to inform you that I will be late.
I'm running 10 min late. Save me a seat!
Pursuant to our arrangement, I shall arrive late.
To whom it may concern: I will be late.

A.text: far too formal for a close friend.

C.text: stiff legal wording that doesn't fit a friend.

D.text: a formal greeting for an unknown reader.

items.stem: Which sentence avoids unnecessary references to personal traits?
items.explanation: Mention traits such as age or gender only when they matter to the point.

options.text: The elderly lady doctor explained the results.
The female doctor, surprisingly, explained the results clearly.
The young male nurse helped the patient.

A.text: age and gender have nothing to do with the point.

B.text: mentions gender, and "surprisingly" implies bias.

C.text: age and gender have nothing to do with the point.

items.stem:
Which choice is the most precise wording for a formal report?

The medication ___ the patient's pain.
items.explanation: "Reduced" is precise and formal.

A.text: vague and informal.

B.text: slang.

C.text: vague and informal.

items.stem:
Choose the best transition for the blank.

The clinic extended its hours. ___, more working adults were able to get care.
items.explanation: The second sentence describes an effect of the first, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

A.text: signals a contrast, but the second sentence is a result.

C.text: the second sentence isn't an example of extended hours.

D.text: signals a comparison, not a result.

items.stem:
Choose the best transition for the blank.

Some students study best in the morning. ___, others focus better at night.
items.explanation: The two sentences describe opposite habits, so a contrast transition fits.

A.text: signals a result; night studying isn't caused by morning studying.

B.text: the second sentence isn't an example of the first.

C.text: signals a result, not a difference.

items.stem:
Which sentence would best conclude this paragraph?

Drinking enough water helps the body in several ways. It keeps body temperature steady. It helps the kidneys remove waste. It also cushions the joints.
items.explanation: A concluding sentence sums up the main idea that the details supported.

options.text: Some people prefer sparkling water to plain tap water.
For these reasons, staying hydrated supports good health.
Water covers most of Earth's surface, including the oceans.
Coffee and tea also contain a lot of water.

A.text: an off-topic detail.

C.text: true, but off topic.

D.text: introduces a new topic instead of wrapping up.

items.stem: Put these sentences in the most logical order for a paragraph about checking a pulse at the wrist.
items.explanation: The steps follow time order: rest first, find the pulse, count, then calculate.

options.text: Place two fingers on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb.
Multiply the count by 2 to get beats per minute.
Have the person sit and rest for a few minutes.

generalNotes: Common error: counting before the fingers are placed. Another: multiplying before counting.

items.stem: A paragraph's topic sentence is "Regular sleep improves student performance." Which sentences support it? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: A, C, and E each connect sleep to learning or test performance.

options.text: Well-rested students remember more of what they study.
Sleep helps the brain store new information.
Some students work night shifts at restaurants.
Students who sleep enough often score higher on tests.

B.text: about furniture, not performance.

D.text: about jobs; it doesn't connect sleep to performance.

items.stem: Which sentence does NOT belong in a paragraph about preparing for a blood draw?
items.explanation: The paragraph is about how to prepare. What blood is made of is true but off topic.

options.text: Drink plenty of water the day before so your veins are easier to find.
Wear a shirt with sleeves that roll up easily.
Blood is made of plasma, red cells, white cells, and platelets.
Tell the technician if you tend to feel faint.

A.text: a preparation tip.

B.text: a preparation tip.

D.text: a preparation tip.

items.stem:
Which topic sentence best fits these supporting details?

• The program offers evening classes.
• Students can get help with child care costs.
• Tutors are available on weekends.
items.explanation: Each detail shows the program fitting around jobs and family, so this main idea covers all three.

options.text: Evening classes in the program start at 6 p.m. on weeknights.
The program is designed to fit the lives of working adults.
Tutoring can be useful for many different kinds of students.
Many college programs in Virginia are expensive to attend.

A.text: a single detail, not a main idea.

C.text: covers only one detail.

D.text: doesn't connect to the details listed.

items.stem: A writer lists reasons to wash hands and saves the strongest reason for last. Which transition best introduces that last reason?
items.explanation: Order of importance builds to the strongest point, often signaled by "most importantly."

B.text: starts a list rather than ending it.

C.text: introduces an example, not the strongest reason.

D.text: signals an opposing idea.

items.stem:
Which method of organization does this paragraph use?

First, blood enters the right atrium. Next, it flows into the right ventricle. Then it is pumped to the lungs.
items.explanation: The signal words first, next, and then show steps in time order.

A.text: describes where things are, not when they happen.

B.text: would show similarities and differences.

D.text: would rank ideas from least to most important.

items.stem: A student lists every idea she can think of about her topic without judging any of them. Which prewriting strategy is she using?
items.explanation: Brainstorming means listing ideas freely before choosing what to use.

B.text: checks a finished draft for errors.

C.text: gives credit to sources.

D.text: improves a draft that already exists.

items.stem: Which task belongs to the drafting stage of the writing process?
items.explanation: Drafting turns the plan into a first full version.

options.text: Writing full paragraphs from an outline
Choosing a topic and making a list of ideas
Checking each sentence for comma errors
Submitting the final copy to the instructor

B.text: prewriting.

C.text: editing.

D.text: publishing.

items.stem:
Which addition would most strengthen support for this thesis?

Community gardens improve neighborhood health.
items.explanation: Data that links gardens to healthier eating directly supports the claim.

options.text: A sentence explaining that the writer personally enjoys gardening
A paragraph describing the history of the garden shovel
Survey data showing garden members eat more vegetables
A list of the most popular flower colors in local gardens

A.text: personal preference isn't evidence.

B.text: off topic.

D.text: doesn't connect to health.

items.stem: Which is the strongest evidence for the claim that handwashing reduces infections?
items.explanation: Data from a study is stronger evidence than opinion or a single anecdote.

options.text: My friend washes her hands all the time and almost never gets sick.
Washing your hands with warm water and soap feels very refreshing.
Everyone already knows that washing your hands works well.
A hospital study found infections fell as staff handwashing rose.

A.text: one person's experience is weak evidence.

B.text: a feeling isn't evidence about infections.

C.text: an appeal to popular belief, not evidence.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of plagiarism?
items.explanation: Using someone else's words or ideas without credit is plagiarism.

options.text: Copying a paragraph from a website without quotation marks or credit
Quoting a source in quotation marks and citing it
Summarizing a source in your own words and citing it
Stating common knowledge, such as "the heart pumps blood," without a citation

B.text: proper use of a source.

C.text: proper use of a source.

D.text: common knowledge doesn't need a citation.

items.stem: While revising, a writer notices that one paragraph discusses two unrelated ideas. What should the writer do?
items.explanation: Each paragraph should develop one main idea, so the two ideas need separate paragraphs.

options.text: Split it into two paragraphs, each with its own topic sentence
Correct all the spelling errors in that paragraph
Add a more interesting title to the beginning of the essay
Delete the conclusion so the essay is shorter

B.text: editing won't fix a problem with unity.

C.text: doesn't address the paragraph.

D.text: unrelated to the problem.

items.stem: In a short academic essay, where is the thesis statement usually placed?
items.explanation: The introduction leads up to the thesis, which tells the reader the essay's main claim.

options.text: At the end of the introduction
In the middle of the second body paragraph

A.text: the conclusion restates the thesis; it doesn't introduce it.

C.text: readers need the main claim up front.

D.text: a title isn't a full thesis statement.

items.stem: During prewriting, which question best helps a writer plan for the audience?
items.explanation: Thinking about readers' needs and background shapes content, word choice, and tone.

options.text: Did I spell every word in my draft correctly?
Which font and color will make the essay look best?
Are all of my commas in the right places?
Who will read this, and what do they already know?

A.text: an editing question.

B.text: about formatting, not audience.

C.text: an editing question.

items.stem:
Which sentence is the best paraphrase of this one?

"Regular exercise lowers the risk of heart disease."
items.explanation: A paraphrase keeps the original meaning in new words.

options.text: "Regular exercise lowers the risk of heart disease."
People who work out often are less likely to develop heart problems.
Exercise is one of the main causes of heart disease in adults.
Heart disease is a common illness in the United States.

A.text: this is a direct quotation, not a paraphrase.

C.text: reverses the meaning.

D.text: drops the main idea about exercise.

items.stem: What is the main job of a conclusion paragraph?
items.explanation: A conclusion wraps up by restating the thesis in new words and showing its significance.

options.text: To restate the main point and show why it matters
To introduce a brand-new argument for the reader
To list every source the writer used in the essay
To apologize for any weaknesses in the argument

B.text: new arguments belong in the body.

C.text: that's the job of the reference list.

D.text: undercuts the essay.

items.stem: Which point would support the thesis "High schools should start later in the morning"?
items.explanation: Only this point gives a reason for the claim.

options.text: Teenagers get more sleep when school starts later.
Later start times can make it harder for students to get to after-school jobs.

A.text: about bus color, not start times.

C.text: about dress codes, not start times.

D.text: on topic, but it's a point against the thesis, not support for it.

items.stem: Why might a writer include a counterargument in a persuasive essay?
items.explanation: Addressing the other side and answering it makes an argument more convincing.

options.text: To confuse readers about which side the writer is on
To make the essay shorter and easier to finish
To answer an opposing view and strengthen the argument
To replace the thesis statement with a new claim

A.text: a counterargument is answered, not left hanging.

B.text: it usually adds length.

D.text: the thesis stays the same.

items.stem: Put the stages of the writing process in order.
items.explanation: Plan (prewriting), write (drafting), improve the content (revising), then fix surface errors (editing and proofreading).
generalNotes: Common error: editing before revising; there's no point polishing sentences that may be cut.

items.stem: Which of these are revising tasks? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: Revising changes content and organization: moving, adding, and cutting.

options.text: Moving a paragraph to improve the order
Adding an example to support a point
Cutting a sentence that is off topic

B.text: fixing spelling and punctuation is editing.

D.text: fixing spelling and punctuation is editing.

items.stem: Which source is most reliable for a research paper on high blood pressure?
items.explanation: Government health agencies publish reviewed, evidence-based information and name their sources.

options.text: An anonymous post shared widely on social media
An advertisement for a blood pressure supplement
An online forum where users share their opinions
A government health agency website, such as the CDC's

A.text: no author or evidence to check.

B.text: written to sell a product.

C.text: opinions, not checked facts.

items.stem: Which detail best supports the thesis "Everyone should learn basic first aid"?
items.explanation: Evidence that bystander CPR saves lives gives a strong reason for everyone to learn it.

options.text: First aid kits come in many sizes and are sold at most drugstores.
The American Red Cross, which teaches first aid, was founded in the 1800s.
Prompt bystander CPR can double or triple the chance of surviving cardiac arrest.
Some people dislike the sight of blood and feel uneasy around injuries.

A.text: doesn't give a reason to learn first aid.

B.text: a history fact, not a reason.

D.text: doesn't support the claim.

items.stem: The prefix brady- means
items.explanation: Brady- means slow, as in bradycardia (a slow heart rate).

A.text: fast is tachy-.

B.text: large or enlarged is megal/o or -megaly.

D.text: pain is -algia.

items.stem: Using its word parts, what does gastritis mean?
items.explanation: Gastr/o = stomach; -itis = inflammation.

A.text: removal is -ectomy (gastrectomy).

B.text: study of is -logy.

C.text: pain is -algia.

items.stem: Which term means surgical removal of the appendix?
items.explanation: -Ectomy means surgical removal.

A.text: -itis means inflammation.

B.text: -otomy means cutting into, not removal.

C.text: -algia means pain.

items.stem: The root nephr/o refers to the
items.explanation: Nephr/o means kidney, as in nephrology.

A.text: liver is hepat/o.

C.text: lung is pulmon/o or pneumon/o.

D.text: nerve is neur/o.

items.stem: Using its word parts, what does intravenous mean?
items.explanation: Intra- = within; ven/o = vein.

A.text: around is peri-.

B.text: under is sub-.

D.text: removal is -ectomy.

items.stem: Using its word parts, what does cardiomegaly mean?
items.explanation: Cardi/o = heart; -megaly = enlargement.

A.text: that's bradycardia.

C.text: that's carditis.

D.text: pain is -algia.

items.stem: The suffix -algia means
items.explanation: -Algia means pain, as in neuralgia (nerve pain).

B.text: inflammation is -itis.

C.text: enlargement is -megaly.

D.text: study of is -logy.

items.stem: Which term means a body temperature that is below normal?
items.explanation: Hypo- = below; therm/o = heat; -ia = condition.

B.text: hyper- means above normal.

C.text: glyc/o means sugar: low blood sugar.

D.text: therm/o = heat and -meter = measuring instrument; a thermometer measures temperature, not a condition.

items.stem: Using its word parts, what does pericardium most likely refer to?
items.explanation: Peri- = around; cardi/o = heart.

options.text: The inside lining of the heart

A.text: inside would be endo- (endocardium).

C.text: muscle is my/o (myocardium).

D.text: that's cardiomegaly.

items.stem: Using its word parts, what does transport mean?
items.explanation: Trans- = across; port = carry.

B.text: "look" is the root spect.

C.text: "write" is the root scrib/script, and "again" is re-.

D.text: "not" is un- or in-, and "able" is -able.

items.stem: What does dys- mean in the word dysfunction?
items.explanation: Dys- means difficult, painful, or abnormal. A dysfunction is abnormal or impaired function.

A.text: without is a- or an-.

B.text: under is sub-.

D.text: again is re-.

items.stem: Which word part means cell?
items.explanation: Cyt/o means cell, as in cytology (the study of cells).

A.text: my/o means muscle.

C.text: oste/o means bone.

D.text: derm/o means skin.

items.stem: A patient reports arthralgia. Using word parts, what does this mean?
items.explanation: Arthr/o = joint; -algia = pain.

A.text: that would be arthritis (-itis).

B.text: removal is -ectomy.

D.text: enlargement is -megaly.

items.stem: In the word postoperative, the prefix post- means
items.explanation: Postoperative means after surgery.

A.text: before is pre-.

B.text: during is intra- (intraoperative).

C.text: around is peri-.

items.stem: Which words contain a word part meaning blood? Select all that apply.
items.explanation: Hemat/o and hem/o mean blood (hematology, hemorrhage); -emia means a blood condition (anemia).

C.text: hepat/o means liver.

items.stem: Which term means the study of the skin?
items.explanation: Dermat/o = skin; -logy = study of.

A.text: -itis means inflammation.

B.text: hemat/o means blood.

C.text: cyt/o means cell.

items.stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
items.explanation: A summary covers the main idea of the whole passage: several theories, none proven.

options.text: Yawning brings extra oxygen to a tired brain, which is why people yawn when they are sleepy.
Scientists have proposed several explanations for yawning, but none has been proven.
Contagious yawning proves that people feel more empathy for strangers than for family members.
Dogs, cats, and fish yawn just as often as humans do, which shows that yawning is very old.

A.text: the passage says this idea "did not hold up."

C.text: reverses the detail (people catch yawns more from family) and overstates it as proof.

D.text: the passage says animals yawn but never compares how often or discusses age.

items.stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
items.explanation: The best summary covers the oysters' main role (filtering water) and the effort to restore them; the other options are single details or misstatements.

options.text: Oysters help clean the bay's water, and people are working to restore them.
A single adult oyster can filter as much as 50 gallons of water in just one day.
Overharvesting was the only reason the bay's oyster population fell sharply.
Underwater grasses in the bay give shelter to young crabs and many kinds of fish.

B.text: a single detail, not the main idea.

C.text: the passage also names disease and pollution.

D.text: a supporting detail, not the main idea.

items.stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
items.explanation: The passage's main point is that Nightingale used careful records and statistics to show that most deaths came from preventable disease, which helped change policy.

options.text: Nightingale helped establish a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London in 1860.
Most soldiers who died in the Crimean War were killed by their wounds from battle.
Nightingale's statistics showed most deaths were preventable and helped bring about reforms.
Nightingale's book Notes on Nursing taught nurses how to draw statistical charts.

A.text: a single detail from the last paragraph.

B.text: contradicts the passage: most died of disease.

D.text: the passage says the book stressed fresh air, clean water, and cleanliness.

items.stem: Which sentence best summarizes the story?
items.explanation: A summary of a story covers its beginning, key event, and outcome.

options.text: A charge nurse hands Dana a clipboard and a list of eight residents to care for.
On her first day, Dana asks why a resident won't eat, gets his problem fixed, and earns praise.
A resident refuses his lunch because he dislikes the food that the kitchen serves him every day.
Dana arrives early but decides by the end of the day that the job is too hard.

A.text: a detail from the opening, not the whole story.

C.text: gives the wrong reason; his dentures hurt.

D.text: contradicts the ending: she looks forward to tomorrow.

items.stem: What can the reader infer from Ms. Okafor's comment at the end of the story?
items.explanation: She praises Dana for noticing something others missed and calls that what the job is "really about."

options.text: She values staff who pay close attention to residents' needs.
She is upset that Dana spent so long talking with Mr. Bell.
She plans to promote Dana to charge nurse right away.
She thinks Dana should have called the kitchen herself.

B.text: her words are praise, not criticism.

C.text: nothing in the story suggests a promotion.

D.text: Ms. Okafor called the kitchen and doesn't criticize Dana for reporting it.

items.stem: According to the brain-cooling explanation, in which situation would a person be LEAST likely to yawn?
items.explanation: The passage says people yawn less when the outside air is very hot, because a deep breath wouldn't cool anything.

options.text: Sitting in a cool room after a long day
Standing outside on a very hot day

A.text: contagious yawning would make a yawn more likely.

B.text: the passage says reading about yawns can trigger one.

C.text: cool air would make a cooling yawn useful.

items.stem: A student parks on campus on January 20 without a spring permit. What will most likely happen?
items.explanation: From January 12 to January 26, vehicles without a permit get a warning; tickets start after January 26.

options.text: The student will receive a warning notice.
The student will receive a $25 ticket.
The student's car will be towed away.
Nothing will happen, because permits are free.

B.text: tickets start after January 26.

C.text: the memo never mentions towing.

D.text: permits being free doesn't mean they're optional.

items.stem: In Story B, why does Mr. Lyle most likely keep planting tomatoes along the fence?
items.explanation: His grumbling that tomatoes grew there "when his wife was alive" suggests habit and memory, not reasons about sunlight.

options.text: He does not know where the sunny corner of the yard is.
His neighbor told him that the fence was the best place in the yard to plant tomatoes.
He is attached to the way things were done when his wife was alive.
He believes tomatoes grow best in the shade.

A.text: he moves the plants there easily once he decides to.

B.text: the neighbor suggested the fence was the problem.

D.text: the story never says this; he says tomatoes "had always grown there."

items.stem: A patient with an 8:00 a.m. fasting test eats a granola bar at 9:30 p.m. the night before. According to the directions, what should the patient do?
items.explanation: The last line says: "If you eat by mistake during the fasting period, call the lab. You may need to reschedule."

options.text: Go to the test as planned without mentioning the snack.
Arrive two hours late so that the fast lasts longer.
Drink extra water to wash out the food before the test.
Call the lab, because the test may need to be rescheduled.

A.text: the directions say to call the lab if you eat by mistake.

B.text: the directions don't offer this option.

C.text: water is allowed, but it doesn't undo eating.

items.stem: According to the label, what should a parent do before giving these tablets to an 8-year-old with hay fever?
items.explanation: For children 6 to under 12 years, the label says "ask a doctor."

options.text: Give half a tablet every 24 hours.
Never use the product for this child.

A.text: that dose is for ages 12 and over.

C.text: the label gives no half-tablet dose.

D.text: "Do not use" applies to children under 6.

items.stem: A person follows the saline-rinse directions but swallows the water after gargling. Which instruction did the person fail to follow?
items.explanation: The directions say: "Spit the water into the sink; do not swallow it."

options.text: Make a fresh mixture each time.
Spit the water into the sink.

A.text: has nothing to do with swallowing.

B.text: has nothing to do with swallowing.

D.text: has nothing to do with swallowing.

items.stem: According to the memo, where can students pick up their parking permits?
items.explanation: Permits are picked up at the Campus Safety office, Room 104, Workforce Building.

options.text: At the visitor spaces near the main entrance

A.text: that's where visitors park.

B.text: the portal is where you fill out the form, not where you pick up the permit.

C.text: the memo doesn't mention a bookstore.

items.stem: According to the passage, in what year did Nightingale publish Notes on Nursing?
items.explanation: The passage says, "In 1859 she published Notes on Nursing."

A.text: the year she arrived at Scutari.

B.text: a year the passage doesn't mention.

D.text: the year the nursing school was established.

items.stem: According to the label, at what temperature should the tablets be stored?
items.explanation: The label says to store the tablets at 68–77 °F.

A.text: much colder than the label's range.

B.text: cooler than the label's range.

D.text: warmer than the label's range.

items.stem: A patient wants a blood draw and a dental cleaning on the same day. On which days is that possible?
items.explanation: Dental cleanings run only on Tuesday and Thursday, and the lab is open both of those mornings.

A.text: dental is closed on both days, and the lab is closed on Wednesday.

C.text: the lab is closed on Wednesday, and dental is closed on both days.

D.text: dental cleanings are closed on Monday and Friday.

items.stem: Which age groups met the health department's goal?
items.explanation: Only the 65+ group (71%) reached at least 70%.

B.text: 50–64 reached only 52%.

C.text: the 65+ group reached 71%, which meets the 70% goal.

D.text: 30–49 reached only 35%.

items.stem: According to the survey, how many more minutes did students who used screens for more than 60 minutes before bed take to fall asleep than students who used no screens?
items.explanation: 41 minutes − 15 minutes = 26 minutes.

A.text: 41 − 30 = 11; this subtracts a screen-time category boundary (30 minutes) instead of the no-screen group's 15 minutes.

B.text: this is the time for the no-screens group.

D.text: this is the total time for the more-than-60-minutes group, not the difference.

items.stem: Which of these events happened first?
items.explanation: She arrived in 1854, during the war; the analysis, book, and school all came later.

options.text: Nightingale helped establish a nursing school in London.
Nightingale worked with statisticians on death rates.
Nightingale arrived at the army hospital in Scutari.

A.text: 1859, after the war.

B.text: 1860, the last event in the passage.

C.text: this happened after the war.

items.stem: What happened immediately after Mr. Bell explained that his dentures hurt?
items.explanation: The order is: Mr. Bell explains → Dana reports → Ms. Okafor calls the kitchen → the soup arrives → he eats.

options.text: Dana reported the problem to Ms. Okafor.
Mr. Bell ate every bite of his meal.
Dana recorded every meal in the chart.

B.text: this happened after Dana reported the problem.

C.text: this happened later, after the soup arrived.

D.text: this happened earlier in the morning.

items.stem: Put these steps for making the saline rinse in the correct order.
items.explanation: The directions say first wash your hands, next pour warm water, then add salt and stir, and then gargle.

options.text: Stir in one-half teaspoon of salt.
Pour warm water into a clean glass.

generalNotes: Common error: adding salt before the water is in the glass. Another: gargling before the salt dissolves.

items.stem: Which sentence from the letter states an opinion?
items.explanation: "Ridiculous" expresses a judgment that can't be proven true or false.

options.text: A 20-ounce bottle of regular soda contains about 16 teaspoons of sugar.
Several hospitals across the country have already stopped selling sugary drinks.
Last week I visited my father at Bayside General Hospital.

A.text: a measurable fact.

B.text: a fact that could be checked.

C.text: a fact about the writer's experience.

items.stem: Which statement in the advertisement is a fact that could be checked?
items.explanation: The amount of an ingredient can be measured and verified.

options.text: Each gummy contains 3 mg of melatonin.
DreamDeep is the most amazing sleep aid ever made.
"I haven't slept this well in years!"

B.text: opinion and exaggeration.

C.text: "harsh" is a judgment word, not a measurable fact.

D.text: one customer's personal opinion, which can't be checked.

items.stem: Which misconception does the advertisement encourage?
items.explanation: The ad says the product is "100% natural, so it is completely safe for everyone." Natural substances can still have side effects and interactions.

options.text: That melatonin is a hormone that plays a role in sleep cycles
That sleeping pills require a prescription
That berry flavors make gummies taste better
That a product labeled natural must be safe for everyone

A.text: this is true, not a misconception, and the ad never mentions it.

B.text: the ad never says this.

C.text: the ad doesn't argue this.

items.stem: Which statement from the letter best shows the writer's bias?
items.explanation: Saying that "every" administrator acts only for profit is an overgeneralization that assumes motives without evidence.

options.text: A 20-ounce bottle of regular soda contains about 16 teaspoons of sugar.
Every hospital administrator who keeps these machines stocked is simply putting profit ahead of patients.
The American Heart Association recommends that most women limit added sugar to about 6 teaspoons a day and most men to about 9.
Several hospitals across the country have already stopped selling sugary drinks.

A.text: a factual statement.

C.text: a factual statement attributed to a named health organization.

D.text: a factual statement.

items.stem: Which statement from the passages is a fact rather than an opinion?
items.explanation: The timing of melatonin release is a scientific finding that can be checked.

options.text: Starting high school at 8:30 a.m. or later is a simple change that protects students' health.
Later start times sound good, but the details matter.
During puberty, the brain begins releasing the sleep hormone melatonin later at night.
Before changing the schedule, our district should study what the change would cost.

A.text: "simple" and the recommendation are judgments.

B.text: a judgment.

D.text: "should" signals a recommendation, not a fact.

items.stem: In the last paragraph, the word humble in "the humble yawn" most nearly means
items.explanation: The author contrasts an everyday, ordinary act with the fact that it is still a mystery.

B.text: the opposite meaning.

C.text: nothing in the passage suggests danger.

D.text: the sentence calls the yawn a mystery, but "humble" describes how ordinary it is.

items.stem: In the last sentence, the word promising most nearly means
items.explanation: Scientists see restoration as a way that will likely improve the bay's health.

A.text: too strong; the passage says restoration takes time.

C.text: the passage doesn't discuss cost.

D.text: the passage says restoration takes time and has gone on for years; "promising" isn't about newness.

items.stem: In the first sentence, the word pioneer most nearly means
items.explanation: Nightingale was among the first to use statistics to change policy.

options.text: one of the first people to do something
a soldier who fought in a war
a person who criticizes the government
a teacher at a nursing school

B.text: she was a nurse, not a soldier.

C.text: the passage describes her persuading officials, not criticizing them.

D.text: she helped establish a school, but "pioneer" refers to being first.

items.stem: In the first paragraph, the word luxury most nearly means
items.explanation: The author says online tutoring is "not a luxury" but a necessity, so luxury means something extra.

options.text: a requirement that every student must meet before graduating
something nice to have but not necessary
a costly mistake that a college later regrets making
a special reward given to students for high grades

A.text: the opposite: the author contrasts luxury with necessity.

C.text: the sentence isn't about mistakes.

D.text: the sentence isn't about rewards.

items.stem: On the label, the word temporarily in "temporarily relieves sneezing" most nearly means
items.explanation: The tablets relieve symptoms for a while, which is why a dose is taken every 24 hours.

A.text: the opposite meaning.

B.text: describes how much, not how long.

D.text: describes speed, not how long.

items.stem: Why does the author most likely end the passage with the question in parentheses?
items.explanation: The question connects to the earlier point that reading about yawns can trigger one, in a light, friendly way.

options.text: To prove that the brain-cooling explanation is correct
To warn readers that frequent yawning is a sign of illness
To playfully show that reading about yawns can cause one
To introduce a new theory that will be explained next

A.text: the passage says none of the explanations is proven.

B.text: the passage never discusses illness.

D.text: it's the last sentence; nothing follows.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the advertisement?
items.explanation: Superlatives, testimonials, and "Order today" show that the goal is to sell.

options.text: To explain the science of how melatonin works
To persuade readers to buy the product
To entertain readers with a story about sleep
To compare several sleep aids fairly

A.text: the ad gives almost no science.

C.text: there's no story.

D.text: it compares only to "harsh sleeping pills," and not fairly.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
items.explanation: Numbered steps and commands such as "Stop eating" show that the purpose is to instruct.

options.text: To tell patients how to prepare for a fasting blood test
To persuade patients that they should get blood tests more often
To explain how labs analyze blood samples
To describe the history of fasting

B.text: it doesn't argue for more tests.

C.text: it doesn't describe lab work.

D.text: it includes no history.

B.text: the opposite of what happened.

C.text: he didn't reject the idea.

items.stem: In the last paragraph, the word monitor in "continue to monitor vaccine safety" most nearly means
items.explanation: Agencies keep checking safety even after approval.

A.text: the sentence says this happens after approval.

B.text: nothing suggests removing vaccines.

C.text: monitoring isn't advertising.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
items.explanation: The passage explains a process in a neutral, informative way.

options.text: To persuade readers to oppose vaccines
To tell a story about a patient getting sick
To explain how vaccines help the immune system
To give directions for scheduling a vaccine

A.text: the passage is not against vaccines.

B.text: there's no story.

D.text: no steps or directions are given.

items.stem: Why does the author include the word PASS?
items.explanation: Each letter stands for a step, making the order easy to recall in an emergency.

options.text: To show that using an extinguisher is a test
To help readers remember the steps in order
To describe how fires start and spread
To list the types of extinguishers sold

A.text: PASS isn't about passing a test.

C.text: it describes using the extinguisher.

D.text: no types are listed.

items.stem: Why does the author describe the rain and the crying toddler?
items.explanation: The story says the class "had not included" these sounds, which explains Marcus's pounding heart.

options.text: To explain how the storm caused the power outage at the clinic
To show why Marcus felt more stress than his class had prepared him for
To show that the toddler was the most seriously ill patient at the clinic that night
To suggest that the clinic should close during bad weather

A.text: the outage's cause isn't the point of these details.

C.text: nothing says the toddler was seriously ill.

D.text: the story doesn't argue this.

items.stem: Why does the author include the last sentence of the passage?
items.explanation: The note explains why steps dipped slightly in May.

options.text: To offer a possible reason for the drop in May
To show that the challenge failed to meet its goal
To argue that employees should not take vacations
To explain how step counters measure steps

B.text: May still met the goal.

C.text: the note doesn't argue this.

D.text: the note is about vacations, not how step counters work.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of a Nutrition Facts label like this one?
items.explanation: The label lists amounts of calories and nutrients per serving so shoppers can compare foods.

options.text: To persuade shoppers that the cereal is the healthiest choice
To give a recipe that uses the cereal as an ingredient
To inform shoppers about what is in one serving of the food
To tell a story about how the cereal was invented

A.text: the label gives facts, not arguments.

B.text: there is no recipe.

D.text: there is no story.

items.stem: The author of Passage B works as an emergency medical technician. How does this most likely shape the author's view?
items.explanation: The author's main reasons are reaching students in emergencies and managing health conditions.

options.text: It makes the author focus on lesson plans and grading.
It makes the author focus on emergencies and medical needs.
It makes the author focus on the cost of new phones.
It makes the author focus on conflicts in the hallway.

A.text: those are a teacher's concerns.

C.text: cost isn't mentioned.

D.text: that's Passage A's concern.

items.stem: The author of Passage A would most likely agree with which statement?
items.explanation: Passage A says even a phone face down "can pull a student's thoughts away."

options.text: Phones should stay in class but be silenced.
Teachers should plan lessons that require students to use their phones.
Phones in class distract students even when they are face down.
Families must be able to text students during class.

A.text: this is closer to Passage B's proposal.

B.text: this is Passage B's point.

D.text: Passage B's concern.

items.stem: From whose perspective is the story mainly told?
items.explanation: The narrator uses "he" and shares Marcus's feelings (his pounding heart, his thoughts on the way home).

options.text: Ms. Reyes's, in the first person
The toddler's mother's, in the first person
The reader's, in the second person

A.text: the story uses "she," not "I," for Ms. Reyes.

B.text: she's described from the outside.

C.text: the story doesn't use "you."

items.stem: Which best describes the author's attitude toward Fleming's discovery?
items.explanation: The title calls it "an accident that changed medicine," and the tone is factual and appreciative.

B.text: the author never makes fun of Fleming.

C.text: the author doesn't criticize Fleming.

D.text: the author states events clearly.

items.stem: Whose interests does the DreamDeep advertisement mainly represent?
items.explanation: An advertisement is written to sell, so it reflects the seller's point of view.

B.text: no doctor is involved.

C.text: the fine print says the FDA hasn't evaluated the claims.

D.text: no research is cited.

items.stem: Based on the passage, what would most likely happen if a vaccinated person were later exposed to the germ the vaccine targets?
items.explanation: The passage says memory cells let the body fight the germ "before you feel ill."

options.text: The person would become sick for several days, exactly as if never vaccinated.
The person's body would have no defense, because vaccines contain dead germs.
The person's memory cells would recognize the germ and fight it quickly.
The person would need a new vaccine before the immune system could respond.

A.text: the vaccine's purpose is to prevent this.

B.text: the passage says vaccines lead to memory cells.

D.text: memory cells already allow a quick response.

items.stem: Suppose that in June employees wear their step counters as often as they did in April. Which prediction is best supported?
items.explanation: When employees wore their counters regularly in April, the average was 7,400 steps, above the 7,000 goal.

options.text: The June average will likely fall back to February's level.
The June average will likely be close to or above the goal.
The company will likely raise the goal to 12,000 steps.
The challenge will likely be cancelled for poor results.

A.text: the passage gives no reason for such a large drop.

C.text: nothing suggests a new goal.

D.text: the results met the goal.

items.stem: Which sentence best supports the conclusion that Fleming's discovery alone was not enough to help patients?
items.explanation: This sentence directly says penicillin couldn't yet be made in usable amounts.

options.text: "Around the mold was a clear ring where the bacteria had died."
"In 1945, Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine."
"Fleming published his findings in 1929, but he could not produce enough pure penicillin to treat patients."
"Today, doctors warn that bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics when these drugs are overused or misused."

A.text: describes the discovery, not its limits.

B.text: describes an honor, not a limitation.

D.text: about today's resistance, not the early limits.

items.stem: Based on the story, how will Marcus most likely act during the next emergency?
items.explanation: The story ends with Marcus thinking about Ms. Reyes's lesson all the way home.

options.text: He will try to stay calm and reassure patients, as he did that night.
He will refuse to work any shifts during bad weather.
He will leave the patients alone and wait for the manager to tell him what to do.
He will ignore the plan and do whatever feels right.

B.text: nothing suggests he wants to avoid storms.

C.text: he learned the value of staying with patients.

D.text: Ms. Reyes says plans help.

items.stem: A worker uses an extinguisher on a small wastebasket fire, and the fire appears to be out. Based on the directions, what should the worker do next?
items.explanation: The directions say to watch the area because a fire can start again, and to report the fire even if you put it out.

options.text: Return to work right away, since the fire is out.
Put the pin back in and store the extinguisher.
Open the windows and wait for the smoke to clear.
Watch the area and report the fire to the fire department.

A.text: the directions say a fire can start again.

B.text: the directions don't mention this.

C.text: the directions don't mention this.

items.stem: Which theme is shared by "The Storm Shift" and "First Shift"?
items.explanation: Both new workers succeed by paying close attention to the people in their care, and each supervisor's closing words stress the importance of people.

options.text: Experienced workers should never trust new employees with important tasks.
Training classes are useless once someone starts a real job.
Bad weather is the greatest danger in health care settings.
A new worker learns that caring attention to people matters most.

A.text: both supervisors trust the new worker with important tasks.

B.text: neither story calls training useless; Marcus's class simply didn't cover everything.

C.text: only one story involves weather.

items.stem: How do the two passages differ in their main concern?
items.explanation: The teacher cites distraction and classroom results; the parent cites emergencies and medical apps.

options.text: Passage A focuses on attention and learning; Passage B focuses on safety and health.
Passage A focuses on emergencies; Passage B focuses on missing assignments.
Both passages focus mainly on the cost of buying phones for students.
Passage A wants phones used in lessons; Passage B wants them banned.

B.text: this reverses the passages.

C.text: neither discusses cost.

D.text: this reverses their positions.

items.stem: On which point would both authors most likely agree?
items.explanation: Passage A wants them in lockers; Passage B wants them silent and out of sight unless a teacher allows them. Both limit free use.

options.text: Phones should be locked away with no exceptions.
Phones should not be used freely during class.
Phones are never useful for learning.
Students' families should not contact them at school.

A.text: Passage B wants medical exceptions.

C.text: Passage B says they can be learning tools.

D.text: Passage B says families need to reach them.

items.stem: How is Fleming's discovery in "An Accident That Changed Medicine" similar to Marisol's success in Story A?
items.explanation: Fleming studied a contaminated dish; Marisol studied her broken bridge.

options.text: Both happened on the very first try without any setbacks.
Both depended on helpful advice that came from a neighbor.
Both came from closely examining something that had gone wrong.
Both ended with a large cash prize for the person who succeeded.

A.text: Marisol failed first, and penicillin took years to develop.

B.text: only Mr. Lyle in Story B got advice.

D.text: neither text mentions money.

items.stem: How is Marcus's situation in "The Storm Shift" different from Marisol's in Story A?
items.explanation: Marcus has to respond in the moment with Ms. Reyes directing him; Marisol studies her broken bridge for a week and redesigns it the next year.

options.text: Marcus fails and never recovers, while Marisol succeeds easily on her very first try.
Marisol works under a supervisor, while Marcus works completely alone during the storm.
Both characters ignore the advice they are given and succeed mostly because of luck.
Marcus must act fast with a supervisor's help; Marisol studies her problem alone over time.

A.text: Marcus handles the night well, and Marisol fails first.

B.text: this reverses the characters.

C.text: neither succeeds by luck, and Marcus follows Ms. Reyes's directions.

items.stem: What evidence does the author of Passage A use to support banning phones in class?
items.explanation: The teacher relies on personal observation of one school's results.

options.text: The teacher's own observations after the school's policy began
Results from a national survey of thousands of teachers in many states
Statements from students who say they prefer phone-free classrooms
Data showing that phone apps help students manage diabetes in class

B.text: the passage cites no survey.

C.text: no students are quoted.

D.text: that's Passage B's point.

items.stem: What is the main weakness of the evidence in Passage A?
items.explanation: Personal observation is useful but limited; it may not apply to other schools.

options.text: It includes too many statistics from scientific studies.
It comes from one teacher's observations at one school.
It focuses only on the cost of the policy.
It relies only on statistics from other schools.

A.text: the passage includes no studies.

C.text: cost isn't discussed.

D.text: the teacher describes only the teacher's own school.

items.stem: Which additional evidence would most strengthen Passage B's argument?
items.explanation: Passage B's main reason is emergencies, so data on emergency use supports it most directly.

options.text: Data showing how often students used phones to reach help during school emergencies
A study showing that phones distract students even when they are face down
A list of schools that require all students to keep their phones in lockers during class
A report showing that most students check social media during class

B.text: this supports Passage A.

C.text: doesn't show the value of phones.

D.text: this supports Passage A.

items.stem: Suppose the company announces that the walking challenge made its employees healthier. What is the main weakness of this conclusion, based on the passage?
items.explanation: Walking more may help health, but the passage measured only steps, so it can't show that health improved.

options.text: The average never reached the company's step goal.
The passage reports step counts, not any measure of health.
The challenge lasted only one week in February.
The wellness coordinator counted every step by hand.

A.text: April and May both met the 7,000-step goal.

C.text: the challenge lasted four months.

D.text: employees wore step counters.

items.stem: Which statement would a critic most likely use to weaken the essay's argument?
items.explanation: Evidence from a single college may not apply everywhere, which is a fair weakness to point out.

options.text: The essay says students study late at night.
The essay's pass-rate data come from only one college.
The essay says good tutors ask guiding questions.
The essay says failing a course costs money.

A.text: this supports the essay.

C.text: this answers a criticism.

D.text: this supports the essay.

items.stem: A student submitted the online permit form on January 8 and wants to pick up the permit as early as possible. The Workforce Building is a short walk from the Student Center stop. Assume January 8 through January 12 are all weekdays and none is a college holiday. Which date and shuttle run from the Main Street Park-and-Ride should the student choose?
items.explanation: The memo says permits are ready starting January 10, and Run 1 is the earliest shuttle to reach the Student Center that day.

options.text: January 9, Run 1 (arrives at the Student Center at 7:35 a.m.)
January 10, Run 2 (arrives at the Student Center at 10:05 a.m.)
January 10, Run 1 (arrives at the Student Center at 7:35 a.m.)
January 12, Run 1 (arrives at the Student Center at 7:35 a.m.)

A.text: January 9 is the form deadline; permits aren't ready until January 10.

B.text: Run 2 is later than Run 1 on the same day.

D.text: January 12 is when permits become required, not the first pickup day.

items.stem: The letter in "Get Sugary Drinks Out of Our Hospital" gives the American Heart Association's daily limit on added sugar for most women. Using the cereal label and that limit, how many servings of the cereal would reach the limit? (1 teaspoon of sugar ≈ 4 grams)
items.explanation: One serving has 8 g of added sugars, which is about 2 teaspoons (8 ÷ 4). The letter gives a limit of about 6 teaspoons for most women, and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 servings.

A.text: compares 8 grams directly with 6 teaspoons without converting units.

B.text: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 is the number of teaspoons in one serving, not the number of servings.

D.text: uses the limit for most men (9 ÷ 2), not for women.

items.stem: Using both passages, which statement is supported?
items.explanation: The vaccine passage explains how vaccines prevent disease, and the walking passage shows average steps rising to meet a goal.

options.text: Both use data tables to show results over several months.
Both argue against the advice given by health agencies.
Both report that their efforts failed to reach their goals in the end.
Both describe ways people can protect or improve their health.

A.text: only the walking passage has a table.

B.text: neither argues against health agencies.

C.text: the challenge met its goal, and the vaccine passage sets no goal.

items.stem: The penicillin passage warns about overusing antibiotics. The fasting-test directions say to take usual medicines unless told to stop. What do both texts suggest about medicines?
items.explanation: One warns against overuse; the other says to follow the provider's instructions. Both point to using medicines as directed.

options.text: They should be stopped whenever a person feels better.
They are always safe in any amount.
They should be used as directed by a health care provider.
They should be avoided before any medical test.

A.text: neither text says this.

B.text: the penicillin passage warns about overuse.

D.text: the directions say to keep taking usual medicines.

items.stem: How could the survey in "Screens and Sleep" be used in the debate about phones in the classroom?
items.explanation: A source is only useful evidence when it measures what the argument is about.

options.text: Neither side could use it directly; it measures bedtime screen use, not class use.
It proves that phones in class cause students to fail their courses.
It shows that students who keep their phones in lockers during class sleep better.
It shows that phones are needed so that students can manage medical conditions.

B.text: the survey doesn't study class time or grades.

C.text: lockers aren't part of the survey.

D.text: the survey says nothing about medical apps.
